Module 7: Immune & Hematologic Disorders

This module covers how blood cells are made and what happens when they go wrong: not enough iron to build red cells (iron deficiency anemia), missing clotting factors (hemophilia), misshapen red cells that block vessels (sickle cell disease), cancerous white cells (leukemia), and a weak immune system (HIV, SCID). Textbook extras add allergies/anaphylaxis, JIA, lupus, and other blood disorders.

🎯

Blueprint focus: pathophysiology, screening, interpreting labs, effects on growth and development, infection prevention, interdisciplinary care, and family teaching for anemia, sickle cell disease, hemophilia, and immune disorders.

Lecture 1: Hematologic Dysfunction, Part 1

Blood basics · Iron deficiency anemia · Hemophilia · Engage Mod 11 & Mod 7
🧬7.1 Blood & Immune Basics: Where Blood Cells Come FromPart 1 slides 2–5 · Textbook

Hematopoiesis (“hema” = blood, “poiesis” = making) is the process of making all blood cells. It happens in the bone marrow, the spongy tissue in the center of bones, where stem cells mature into three families of cells: red blood cells (RBCs) that carry oxygen, white blood cells (WBCs) that fight infection, and platelets that plug leaks and start clots.

🔴 Erythrocytes (RBCs)
Donut-shaped cells with no nucleus, packed with hemoglobin (Hgb), the iron-containing protein that grabs oxygen in the lungs and drops it off in the tissues. They make up about 40–45% of blood volume and live roughly 120 days (about 4 months).
⚪ Leukocytes (WBCs)
  • Neutrophils: first responders that eat bacteria; low count = neutropenia
  • Lymphocytes: B cells make antibodies; T cells kill infected cells and direct the response (CD4 “helper” T cells are what HIV attacks)
  • Monocytes: become macrophages that clean up debris
  • Eosinophils: rise with allergies and parasites
  • Basophils: release histamine in allergic reactions
Erythropoiesis: how the body makes more red cells

When tissues don’t get enough oxygen (hypoxia), the kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone that tells the bone marrow to make more RBCs. To build healthy, well-formed RBCs, the marrow needs enough iron, vitamin B12, folic acid, cobalt, and nickel. If one of these raw materials is missing (iron is the most common), the marrow makes cells that are small and pale, which is the picture of iron deficiency anemia.

Normal pediatric blood values (from the slide)
AgeHgbHct (%)WBCPlatelets
2 months9–14 g/dL28–425,000–19,000150,000–400,000
6–12 years11–15 g/dL35–455,000–15,500150,000–400,000
12–18 years (male)13–16 g/dL37–494,500–13,500150,000–400,000
12–18 years (female)12–16 g/dL36–464,500–13,500150,000–400,000

Hct (hematocrit) is the percentage of blood volume made of RBCs. Notice the 2-month-old’s Hgb can be as low as 9 g/dL and still be normal; this is the expected physiologic nadir, when fetal red cells are breaking down faster than new ones are made. Platelets are 150,000–400,000 at every age, which makes them easy to memorize.

Hemostasis: how the body stops bleeding
  • Blood vessels constrict to slow blood flow.
  • Platelets adhere and aggregate (stick together) to form a soft temporary plug. This is primary hemostasis.
  • Clotting factors are triggered in a chain reaction called the coagulation cascade. Most factors are made in the liver; factor VIII is made by the lining of blood vessels.
  • Prothrombin converts to thrombin, and thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin, a sticky mesh that locks the platelet plug into a firm clot. This is secondary hemostasis.
The immune system in brief (Engage Mod 7)

Innate immunity is what you’re born with: skin, mucous membranes, neutrophils, and macrophages that attack any invader. Adaptive immunity is learned: B and T lymphocytes recognize a specific germ and remember it (the reason vaccines work). Key organs include the bone marrow (where B and T cells form), the thymus (where T cells mature), the spleen (filters blood and removes old RBCs), lymph nodes (filters that trap germs), and Peyer’s patches (guard the intestines). Expected CD4 helper T cell range is about 500–1,500 cells/mm³.

💡 Exam tip
Know the job of each cell: RBC = oxygen, WBC = infection, platelet = clotting. Then every disorder in this module makes sense: anemia = not enough oxygen carriers, leukemia and neutropenia = infection risk, hemophilia and low platelets = bleeding risk.
🥩7.2 Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA): Causes & CluesPart 1 slides 6–8 · Textbook

Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common anemia and most common blood disorder in children worldwide. Iron is the part of hemoglobin that holds oxygen. The body stores extra iron in the liver as ferritin, so the first thing to fall is the ferritin “savings account.” Once stores are empty, the marrow can’t make enough Hgb, RBCs become small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic), and the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity drops.

Only about 30% of daily iron comes from diet; the rest is recycled from old RBCs. Full-term babies are born with iron stores that last about 4–6 months; after that, iron must come from food or formula.

⚠️ Why it matters
Untreated IDA can cause growth restriction and developmental delays. The brain is very sensitive to iron, so IDA is linked to poor attention, learning problems, slower visual and auditory processing, and lower school performance, and the effects can be permanent if severe and early.
Risk factors (slide 8)
Risk factorWhy it causes IDA
Premature birth or low birth weightMost iron transfers from mother to fetus in the third trimester, so preemies start life with small stores.
Excessive cow’s milkCow’s milk is low in iron, blocks iron absorption, fills the child up so they eat fewer iron-rich foods, and can cause tiny hidden GI bleeds, especially before age 1 (“milk babies”).
Chronic diarrheaIron isn’t absorbed and may be lost through the gut.
Poor dietary ironExclusive breastfeeding past 4–6 months without supplements, low-iron formula, picky eating, vegan/vegetarian diets without planning.
Periods of rapid growthInfancy (6 months–3 years) and adolescence: iron needs outrun intake.
Blood lossHeavy menstrual periods in teens, GI bleeding.
Infection and chronic disordersInflammation blocks iron use; folate deficiency, sickle cell anemia, and hemophilia also raise risk.
Clinical manifestations

Many children with mild IDA have no symptoms. When present, think about what happens when tissues are short on oxygen:

🎨 Skin
Pallor (pale skin, lips, conjunctivae), brittle spoon-shaped nails in severe cases.
❤️ Cardiopulmonary
Tachycardia (the heart beats faster to move the little oxygen there is), murmur, tachypnea and shortness of breath with exertion.
🧠 Neurologic
Fatigue, irritability, poor attention, decreased school performance, restless leg syndrome, headache.
👅 Other clues
Pica (craving nonfood items like ice, dirt, chalk), glossitis (sore, smooth tongue), stomatitis (mouth sores), frequent infections.
Labs: what they show in IDA
TestWhat it measuresIn IDA
Hgb / HctOxygen-carrying protein / % of blood that is RBCs↓
Serum ferritinIron stores (the savings account)↓ (the earliest and most specific sign)
Serum iron and transferrin saturationIron circulating in the blood / how full the iron “taxis” (transferrin) are↓
TIBC (total iron-binding capacity)How many empty seats the iron taxis have↑ (the body makes more transport to grab any iron it can)
MCV (mean corpuscular volume)Average size of each RBC↓ (microcytic)
MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin)Average amount (weight) of Hgb in each RBC↓
MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration)Hgb relative to cell size (how “red” the cell is)↓ (hypochromic, pale)
Reticulocyte countYoung RBCs just released from marrow (marrow output)↓ or inappropriately normal; it rises within days once iron is given

Screening: the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends a risk assessment at well-child visits starting at 4 months and a CBC (complete blood count) around 9–12 months, with repeat testing for higher-risk children. A focused diet history is a better predictor than a single Hgb.

💡 Exam tip
“Everything is low except TIBC.” In IDA, Hgb, Hct, ferritin, serum iron, MCV, MCH, and MCHC drop; TIBC rises.
🍊7.3 IDA Treatment, Teaching & Iron SafetyPart 1 slide 9 · Textbook
Dietary changes (slide 9)
  • Encourage breastfeeding, but give breastfed full-term infants an iron supplement starting at 4 months (breastfed preemies start by 2 weeks). Never discourage breastfeeding because of IDA risk.
  • Recommend iron-fortified formula for formula-fed infants for the whole first year (no low-iron formula, no cow’s milk before 12 months).
  • Older children: high-iron foods + vitamin C + protein. Vitamin C (citrus, berries, tomatoes, broccoli) helps the gut absorb iron.
  • Restrict milk to no more than 1 quart (32 oz) a day per the slide. Many references now teach 16–24 oz/day for toddlers; either way, the goal is to stop milk from replacing iron-rich food.
Recommended daily iron (textbook)
AgeRecommended dietary allowance
Full-term infants1 mg/kg/day (max 15 mg)
Premature infants2–4 mg/kg/day (max 15 mg)
1–3 years7 mg/day
4–8 years10 mg/day
9–13 years8 mg/day
Heme iron (animal, absorbed best)Nonheme iron (plant, absorbed better with vitamin C)
Red meat, poultry, seafood/fatty fish, eggsIron-fortified cereals, tofu, beans and lentils, dark green leafy vegetables
Medications

Oral iron (ferrous sulfate) is first-line, usually as elemental iron once daily. How to give it so it works and is safe:

  • Give on an empty stomach or between meals, ideally with vitamin C (orange juice). Do not give with milk, dairy, eggs, cereal, tea, or antacids, which block absorption.
  • Liquid iron stains teeth: use a dropper or straw placed toward the back of the mouth and brush teeth afterward.
  • Use an oral syringe or medicine cup, never a kitchen spoon, and don’t hide it in a full bottle or a favorite food (food aversion).
  • Side effects: dark green-black stools (expected, harmless), constipation, nausea, abdominal pain. Report clay-colored or red stools.
  • Response: reticulocytes rise within days; Hgb should rise by at least 1 g/dL within about 4 weeks (2 weeks if severe). Continue for several months after Hgb normalizes to refill stores.
☠️ Iron poisoning
Iron overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6. Teach: keep iron (including adult prenatal vitamins) locked and out of reach, never call it candy, and don’t double a missed dose.
📝 Note: slide vs. common practice
The slide lists “Interferon – IM Z-track injections” under IDA medications. For your exam, recognize that wording from the slide. In common practice, though, the injectable given IM by Z-track for iron deficiency is parenteral iron (iron dextran, InFeD), not interferon (an immune-modulating drug that isn’t used to treat anemia). Z-track technique is used because iron stains the skin and irritates tissue: pull the skin aside, inject deep into a large muscle, wait 10 seconds, release, and don’t massage. Today, when oral iron fails or can’t be absorbed, IV iron ordered by hematology or GI is more common than IM.
Effects on the whole child

Fatigue and low exercise tolerance can keep a child from sports and play; teach them to rest when tired. IDA lowers immunity, so encourage handwashing and avoiding sick contacts. Picky eating often begins around age 2: keep offering a variety of foods (it can take 10–20 tries), don’t force meals, and involve older kids in meal prep. Budget-friendly iron sources include eggs, beans, and lentils.

💡 Exam tip
Iron teaching on ATI almost always tests: with juice, not milk; straw or back of the mouth; black stools are expected; lock it up.
🩹7.4 Hemophilia: Types, Inheritance & SignsPart 1 slides 10–13 · Textbook

Hemophilia is a group of inherited bleeding disorders in which a clotting factor is missing or doesn’t work. Platelets still make the first soft plug, but without the factor the cascade can’t build a strong fibrin clot, so bleeding lasts longer (it isn’t faster) and can restart after it seems to stop.

TypeMissing factorKey facts
Hemophilia A (“classic”)Factor VIIIAbout 80% of cases. X-linked recessive.
Hemophilia B (“Christmas disease”)Factor IXX-linked recessive; usually less severe than A.
von Willebrand disease (vWD)von Willebrand factor (vWF), the protein that helps platelets stick and carries factor VIIIMost common inherited bleeding disorder overall (about 1 in 1,000). Autosomal, so boys and girls are affected equally. Mucous-membrane bleeding: nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods (over half of females with vWD).
Inheritance: X-linked recessive

The factor VIII and IX genes are on the X chromosome. A boy has only one X, so one affected X = hemophilia. A girl has two X’s, so the healthy X usually covers for the affected one, making her a carrier (some carriers have mild bleeding). A carrier mother has a 50% chance of passing the gene with each pregnancy: each son has a 50% chance of hemophilia and each daughter a 50% chance of being a carrier. An affected father passes the gene to all daughters (carriers) and no sons. About 30% of cases are new mutations with no family history.

Severity depends on factor level
SeverityFactor activityBleeding pattern
Mild5–40%Bleeds after surgery, dental work, or major injury
Moderate1–5%Bleeds after minor injury
SevereLess than 1%Spontaneous bleeds into joints and muscles
Manifestations (slide 12)
  • Prolonged bleeding from any cut or procedure
  • Hemorrhage from any trauma, even losing a baby tooth
  • Newborn: bleeding after circumcision or heel stick is often the first clue
  • Subcutaneous and intramuscular hemorrhage: easy bruising, large hematomas; infants may show irritability or not moving a limb
  • Hemarthrosis (bleeding into a joint) is the most common bleed: knees, elbows, ankles become warm, swollen, stiff, and painful. Repeated bleeds damage cartilage and bone, causing bony changes and crippling.
  • Spontaneous hematuria (blood in urine), nosebleeds, GI bleeding (dark stools)
🚨 Most dangerous bleed
Intracranial bleeding can be fatal. Any head injury, headache, vomiting, irritability, drowsiness, or change in level of consciousness in a child with hemophilia = give factor and get emergency evaluation. Also urgent: neck/throat bleeds (airway) and abdominal bleeds.
💉7.5 Hemophilia: Diagnosis, Management & Nursing CarePart 1 slides 14–17 · Textbook
Diagnosis (slide 14)
  • Based on a history of an excessive bleeding event and family history (X-linked inheritance)
  • Prolonged PTT (partial thromboplastin time, also written aPTT), which tests the pathway that uses factors VIII and IX
  • Factor assays show low factor VIII or IX
  • Platelet count, PT (prothrombin time), and fibrinogen are normal; this pattern separates hemophilia from platelet disorders and DIC
  • Carrier detection by DNA testing; prenatal diagnosis by amniocentesis
💡 Lab pattern to memorize
Hemophilia = only the PTT is long. Everything else (platelets, PT, fibrinogen, bleeding time) is normal. vWD = PTT may be long and platelet function/bleeding time is abnormal.
Management (slide 15)
TreatmentHow it helps / nursing points
Factor replacement (recombinant factor VIII or IX IV)The main treatment. Given for a bleed or on a schedule (prophylaxis) to prevent joint damage. Children and parents are taught to give it at home; school-age kids can learn self-infusion. Watch for inhibitors (antibodies that make factor stop working).
Desmopressin (DDAVP)A synthetic hormone that releases stored factor VIII and vWF. Used for mild hemophilia A and type 1 vWD (doesn’t help hemophilia B). IV or nasal spray. Causes water retention: limit fluids 18–24 hours and watch for hyponatremia (headache, confusion, seizures).
Aminocaproic acid (Amicar) / tranexamic acidAntifibrinolytics: they prevent clot destruction. Very useful for mouth and dental bleeding.
Corticosteroids and NSAIDsUsed with caution: steroids for joint inflammation; NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) and aspirin are avoided because they block platelets. Acetaminophen is the safe choice for pain/fever.
TransfusionsMay be needed for large blood loss, but carry exposure risks (bloodborne infections, reactions). Vaccinate for hepatitis A and B.
Exercise and physical therapyStrong muscles protect joints. After a joint bleed, PT restores motion and prevents contractures.
Hormone therapy or IUD (intrauterine device)For girls and women with vWD to control heavy menstrual bleeding.
Prognosis (slide 16)

In the past, children with severe hemophilia often died by 5 years of age. With factor replacement, they now live nearly normal lives. Gene therapy is the future (and is now beginning).

Nursing care (slide 17)
🛡️ Prevent bleeding
  • Dental procedures in a controlled situation (factor beforehand); soft toothbrush
  • Shave with an electric razor only
  • Avoid IM injections and rectal temperatures when possible; vaccines: smallest gauge (about 23 G) subcutaneous or IM per protocol, then firm pressure about 5 minutes (vWD: about 2 minutes) and ice; one injection at a time
  • No aspirin or NSAIDs; medical alert bracelet
  • Padded furniture corners, helmets and knee/elbow pads; noncontact sports (swimming, biking, walking). Avoid football, hockey, lacrosse, rugby, and heavy lifting
🩹 Recognize and control bleeding
  • Apply firm pressure for 15 minutes or more with ice (slide); ice causes vasoconstriction
  • RICE: rest, ice, compression, elevation; immobilize the joint during a bleed
  • Give factor as soon as possible, before the bleed gets big
  • For mouth/face bleeding, sit the child up
  • After the acute bleed, gradual exercise and PT

Support the patient and family: manage pain (acetaminophen, positioning), support mobility, promote normal growth and development, and prepare for home care (teaching infusions, recognizing bleeds, when to call). Parents may become overprotective; a child needs some age-appropriate risk to develop normally. Teens may react with anger or denial and need help talking to friends and dating partners about their diagnosis.

💡 Exam tip
First action for a joint bleed: factor replacement plus RICE (immobilize, ice, elevate). Never heat, never ibuprofen, never aspirin.

Lecture 2: Hematologic Dysfunction, Part 2: Sickle Cell Disease

Slides 1–20 · Engage Mod 11
🧬7.6 Sickle Cell Disease: Incidence, Inheritance & PathophysiologyPart 2 slides 2–6
Incidence (slide 2)
FactNumber
Americans living with sickle cell anemiaAbout 100,000
Babies born with SCD in the U.S. each yearAbout 1,000
African American births with SCD1 in 365
Hispanic American births with SCD1 in 16,300
African Americans who carry the trait1 in 13
People carrying the sickle cell traitAbout 3 million

The slide’s family diagram shows two carrier parents (AS × AS) and their four possible children: one AA (normal), two AS (carriers), and one SS (sickle cell anemia).

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the most common inherited blood disorder. It is autosomal recessive: a child must inherit a sickle gene (S) from both parents to have the disease. It is most common in people of African descent, and also in Hispanic (Central/South American), Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Indian, and Asian ancestry.

GenotypeNameWhat it means
AAUnaffectedNormal hemoglobin
AS (heterozygous)Sickle cell trait (carrier)Usually no symptoms; can pass the gene
SS (homozygous)Sickle cell anemia (disease)Symptomatic; the most common and severe form

Two carrier parents (AS × AS): each pregnancy has a 25% chance of SS (disease), 50% AS (trait), and 25% AA. There are different sickle cell diseases (for example, hemoglobin SC disease and sickle beta-thalassemia) depending on which abnormal genes combine.

Diagnosis (slide 4)
  • Newborn metabolic screen: universal in the U.S.
  • Hemoglobin electrophoresis: separates the types of hemoglobin; the only definitive postnatal test
  • Peripheral blood smear: shows sickled cells
  • Prenatal testing: amniocentesis or placental sampling
  • Diagnosis is definitive after 6 months of age. Newborns are protected by fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which doesn’t sickle; symptoms usually start around 6 months as HbF fades.
Pathophysiology (slide 5)
  • A single substitution on the beta chain of hemoglobin creates hemoglobin S (HbS).
  • When oxygen is low or blood becomes thick (increased viscosity, as with dehydration), HbS clumps and bends the RBC into a sickle shape.
  • Sickled cells are stiff, clump together, and plug small vessels → tissue ischemia (lack of blood flow), infarction (tissue death), and severe pain.
  • Sickled cells are destroyed quickly: they live only 10–20 days instead of 120 → chronic hemolytic anemia and jaundice.
  • Sickling episodes are called crises. Three major types: vaso-occlusive, sequestration, and aplastic.
💡 Exam tip
Anything that lowers oxygen or thickens blood triggers sickling: dehydration, infection/fever, cold, high altitude, stress, strenuous exercise. Hydration and oxygenation are the backbone of every intervention.
⚡7.7 Sickle Cell Crises & Acute Chest SyndromePart 2 slides 6–12
1. Vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC): the most common

Sickled cells block blood flow, so tissue beyond the block is starved of oxygen. It can be acute or chronic and is triggered by stress, infection, and decreased oxygen (plus dehydration and cold). Severity depends on the site. The classic first crisis in infants and toddlers is dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome): painful, symmetric swelling of the hands and feet. Other sites: bones, abdomen, chest, and brain (stroke). Priapism (painful sustained erection) is a urologic emergency.

The slide’s VOC diagram traces the path: stressor → RBC with HbS → sickled RBC → multi-system effect:

Body systemEffect of vaso-occlusion
CNS (central nervous system)Decreased coordination and sensation, paralysis (stroke)
MusculoskeletalDecreased growth, pain, hand-and-foot syndrome
LungsPneumonia, infection (acute chest syndrome)
LiverJaundice
KidneyHematuria
2. Splenic sequestration crisis: the deadliest

Large amounts of blood suddenly pool in the spleen (and sometimes the liver), which leads to vascular collapse and circulatory shock (slide 9). It is seen only in young children (about 6 months to 4 years), before the spleen scars down. The child develops hypovolemia leading to cardiovascular collapse: a rapidly enlarging spleen (left upper abdominal fullness), sudden pallor, weakness, tachycardia, and hypotension. Treatment: blood transfusions and fluids; possible surgery (splenectomy), since more than 50% of survivors have another episode. Teach parents to palpate the spleen and seek care immediately if it enlarges.

3. Aplastic crisis

Because sickled RBCs already live such a short time, if the bone marrow shuts down even briefly, the child develops profound anemia. It is usually secondary to a viral infection, especially parvovirus B19 (fifth disease). Lasts 7–10 days, rarely recurs, and the marrow usually recovers on its own; transfusion supports the child until it does. Clue: very low Hgb with a low reticulocyte count.

Acute chest syndrome (ACS)

Sickle cells block blood vessels in the lungs, often together with lung infection. It causes chest pain, fever, cough, difficulty breathing, and low oxygen (hypoxemia), can lead to pulmonary hypertension, and is life-threatening and requires emergency care. The slide notes it mainly affects adults and can be fatal, but it is also a leading cause of death and ICU admission in children with SCD. Prevention in the hospital: incentive spirometry, adequate pain control so the child breathes deeply, hydration without overloading, and early mobility.

Other complications to know

Infection is a leading cause of death in young children because the spleen stops working (functional asplenia, eventually “autosplenectomy”): a fever of 38.5°C (101.3°F) or higher is an emergency. Stroke (watch for weakness, speech changes, seizures; screening with transcranial Doppler). Gallstones from constant hemolysis. Hyposthenuria: kidneys can’t concentrate urine, so the child voids large amounts of dilute urine, may wet the bed, and dehydrates easily. Delayed growth and puberty.

💡 Exam tip
Match the crisis to its clue: VOC = pain/swelling · sequestration = big spleen + shock (6 months–4 years) · aplastic = parvovirus + very low Hgb/retic · ACS = chest pain, fever, hypoxia.
🌡️7.8 Sickle Cell Nursing Care, Treatment & TeachingPart 2 slides 13–20 · Kyla case
Nursing assessment (slide 13)
  • Pain intensity and location with an age-appropriate scale (FACES for young children, numeric scale for older children); believe the child’s report
  • Swelling of joints and the periphery (hands and feet)
  • Weakness and fatigue
  • Pallor, tachycardia, altered LOC (level of consciousness), hypotension: signs of severe anemia or sequestration/shock
  • Fever and irritability: infection or ACS
  • Respiratory status and SpO₂ (oxygen saturation), neuro checks for stroke, spleen size
Treatment of vaso-occlusive crisis (slide 14)
🛏️ Acute care
  • Bed rest to reduce oxygen demand
  • Fluid therapy (IV and oral) to thin the blood, usually about 1.5 times maintenance; avoid big boluses that can cause pulmonary edema
  • Analgesics on a schedule, not just as needed: opioids such as morphine, often by PCA (patient-controlled analgesia); NSAIDs such as ketorolac or ibuprofen; acetaminophen
  • Antibiotics to treat any infection
  • Oxygen when there is respiratory distress or hypoxemia
  • Packed RBC transfusion for severe anemia
  • Splenectomy to prevent recurrent sequestration
💊 Long-term therapy
  • Hydroxyurea: raises fetal hemoglobin (HbF) so fewer cells sickle; fewer crises and ACS. Causes bone marrow suppression, so CBCs are monitored.
  • Endari (L-glutamine): oral powder that reduces oxidative stress in RBCs; fewer pain crises.
  • Crizanlizumab and voxelotor (textbook): newer drugs that reduce crises.
  • CRISPR gene editing (Casgevy) and gene therapy using the child’s own hematopoietic stem cells (Lyfgenia), for age 12 and older
  • Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT): the only other cure; used for severe disease
Nursing interventions during a crisis (slide 15)
  • Careful I&O (intake and output) and increase fluids; daily weights
  • Antibiotics as ordered; blood cultures for fever
  • Pulse oximetry; oxygen only if hypoxemic (oxygen doesn’t reverse sickling and can suppress marrow if overused)
  • Pain management (morphine), reassessed after each dose
  • No cold (use warmth): never use ice packs; cold causes vasoconstriction and more sickling. Warm compresses help.
  • Bed rest with passive ROM (range of motion)
  • HOB (head of bed) up to ease breathing
  • Family and child support; child life, school plans
Patient education (slide 16)
🚫 Avoid
  • Strenuous activity and contact sports
  • Emotional stress
  • High altitudes (mountains, unpressurized planes)
  • Known sources of infection
  • Dehydration
  • Heat and cold stress (swimming in cold water, hot outdoor games)
✅ Promote
  • Hydration every day, more with heat or exercise
  • Adequate nutrition and rest
  • Immunizations on schedule plus pneumococcal and yearly flu vaccines
  • Prophylactic penicillin daily, usually until at least age 5
  • Following the medication regimen
  • Low-intensity exercise as tolerated with breaks
  • Fever of 38.5°C (101.3°F) or higher → go to the hospital
Case scenario: Kyla (slides 17–20)

Kyla, 12, has SCD and is having more frequent crises since adolescence. After a lacrosse game on a summer day she has severe generalized pain. Vital signs: T 37.6°C (99.7°F), HR 118, RR 33, BP 96/70, SpO₂ 89%. Labs: Hgb 9, Hct 24%, WBC 12,000, platelets 14,000.

🤔 What are your impressions, priorities, and teaching for Kyla?
  • Impressions: a vaso-occlusive crisis triggered by strenuous exercise, heat, and likely dehydration; tachycardia and tachypnea with SpO₂ 89% raise concern for acute chest syndrome. Anemia is present, and the very low platelet count adds bleeding risk.
  • Priorities: oxygenation first (O₂ to keep SpO₂ at goal, HOB up, incentive spirometry), IV hydration, scheduled analgesia (morphine/PCA), monitor respiratory status, I&O, daily weight, temperature; bleeding precautions; warmth, not ice.
  • Teaching before discharge: hydrate before, during, and after sports; avoid heat/cold extremes and exhaustion; take rests; take hydroxyurea and other meds as prescribed; recognize early ACS and fever; vaccines; talk with coaches and school; begin taking ownership of her care as she moves toward adult care.
💡 Exam tip
Most common ATI traps: ice on a painful joint (wrong; use warmth), “give oxygen to stop sickling” (only if hypoxemic), and forgetting that hydration is the first-line intervention for VOC.
🎗️

Lecture 3: Hematologic Dysfunction, Part 3: Leukemia & Immune Deficiency

Slides 1–18 · Engage Mod 11 & Mod 7
🧫7.9 Leukemia: Types, Signs & DiagnosisPart 3 slides 2–8 · Isla case
Case scenario: Isla (slides 2–3)

Isla, 6, has been more tired for a few weeks, is falling asleep in school, has prolonged nosebleeds, and bruises on her legs and arms she can’t explain. Her mucous membranes are very pale. CBC: WBC 40,000 (high, mostly immature cells), platelets 80,000 (low), Hgb 12.8, Hct 32% (low). Bone marrow confirmed leukemia, and chemotherapy started the next day.

Leukemia is cancer of the blood-forming tissue. The bone marrow overproduces immature WBCs called blasts that never learn to do their job. These blasts crowd out normal marrow, so the child ends up short on everything else. It is classified by which type of WBC is cancerous:

Acute lymphoblastic/lymphoid leukemia (ALL)Acute myelogenous (nonlymphoid) leukemia (AML)
Cell involvedLymphoid line (immature lymphocytes)Myeloid line (cells that become granulocytes, monocytes, RBCs, platelets)
How commonMost common childhood cancer (about 75–80% of childhood leukemia)About 15–20% of childhood leukemia
Survival (slide)About 80% (now often higher)About 45–50%
NotesPeak age 2–6 years; more common in boys older than 1; higher risk with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)Linked to radiation, prior chemo, Down syndrome; CNS signs (headache, facial nerve palsy) more often
Why the symptoms happen: three cell lines crowded out
Missing normal cellResultWhat you see
RBCsAnemiaPallor, fatigue, listlessness, tachycardia
Mature WBCs (neutrophils)NeutropeniaFever, frequent infections
PlateletsThrombocytopeniaBruising, petechiae (tiny red-purple dots), nosebleeds, gum bleeding
Manifestations (slides 6–7)
Early: history and physical
  • Anorexia, headache, fatigue, listlessness
  • Low-grade fever
  • Pallor
  • Increased bruising and petechiae
  • Enlarged liver, spleen, and lymph nodes; swollen joints
  • Bone, leg, and joint pain (the marrow is packed); a child may limp or refuse to walk
  • Abdominal pain, nausea, constipation
  • Increased immature WBCs
Late
  • Hematuria
  • Ulcerations in the mouth
  • Enlarged kidneys and testicles (leukemic infiltration)
  • Enlarged organs
  • Signs of increased intracranial pressure (CNS spread): headache, vomiting, irritability
  • Deficient RBCs → anemia; mature WBCs → neutropenia; platelets → thrombocytopenia
Diagnostics (slide 8)
  • History and physical exam
  • CBC with differential: immature leukocytes (blasts); WBC may be high, normal, or low
  • Lumbar puncture: checks for leukemic cells in the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid); the CNS is a hiding place for leukemia
  • Sonograms: liver and spleen infiltration, enlargement, and fibrosis
  • Bone marrow aspiration or biopsy confirms the diagnosis: done under local and/or general anesthesia (sedation for children); specimen from the posterior iliac crest (or tibia in infants); apply pressure 5–10 minutes afterward; rest for 24 hours; watch the site for bleeding and infection.
💡 Exam tip
The leukemia triad = pale and tired (anemia), fever and infections (neutropenia), bruises and nosebleeds (thrombocytopenia), often with bone pain. Bone marrow biopsy is the definitive test.
🛡️7.10 Leukemia Treatment, Chemo Complications & NeutropeniaPart 3 slides 9–14 · Textbook
Management (slide 9)
  • Chemotherapeutic agents in phases: induction (aims for remission), consolidation/CNS prophylaxis, and maintenance (2–3 years for ALL). Side effects you’ll manage: mucosal irritation (mouth sores), skin breakdown, neuropathy (tingling, constipation, foot drop, especially with vincristine), loss of appetite, hemorrhagic cystitis (bloody bladder irritation from cyclophosphamide: push fluids, void often), and alopecia (hair loss).
  • Cranial irradiation (the slide says “clinical irradiation”) for CNS disease
  • Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) for high-risk or relapsed leukemia
  • Chemo needs a central line or implanted port: sterile access with a non-coring needle, monitor for infection
Complications of chemo and nursing care (slides 10–11)
ProblemWhyNursing actions
Infection (the #1 cause of death during treatment)Chemo and leukemia destroy neutrophilsPrivate room, restrict visitors (no one who is ill), strict handwashing, assess potential sites (mouth, skin, IV/port sites, perianal area, lungs), give antibiotics promptly (fever with neutropenia = emergency; broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour), monitor the ANC, encourage protein for healing. No rectal temps, suppositories, or enemas. No live vaccines, fresh flowers, or standing water.
BleedingLow plateletsMonitor for petechiae, bruising, nosebleeds, blood in urine/stool; avoid unnecessary skin punctures; administer platelets as ordered; soft toothbrush; no NSAIDs or aspirin; avoid contact sports.
AnemiaLow RBCsBlood transfusion (packed RBCs), allow rest and cluster care, oxygen, IV therapy for hydration.
Long-term effectsLate effects of chemo/radiationCardiotoxicity (from anthracyclines like doxorubicin), delayed growth and development, learning problems, infertility, second cancers. Lifelong survivor follow-up.
Absolute neutrophil count (ANC)

The ANC tells you how many infection-fighting neutrophils the child really has. ANC = total WBC × (% neutrophils + % bands) ÷ 100. Example: WBC 2,000 with 10% neutrophils and 5% bands → 2,000 × 15 ÷ 100 = 300.

ANCMeaning
More than 1,500Normal
1,000–1,500Mild neutropenia
500–1,000Moderate neutropenia
Less than 500Severe: protective (neutropenic) precautions
HSCT risks and prognosis (slides 12–13)

HSCT has a significant risk of illness and death: graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), where the donor’s immune cells attack the child’s skin, gut, and liver (rash, diarrhea, jaundice); overwhelming infection; and severe organ damage. Cure after stem cell transplant is about 60–70%. If relapse occurs after HSCT, prognosis is dismal. Factors that predict prognosis: initial WBC at diagnosis (lower is better; over 50,000 is higher risk), age at diagnosis (2–10 years is best; under 1 or over 10 is worse), type of cell, gender (girls do slightly better), and karyotype (chromosome analysis of the cancer cells).

Increased susceptibility to infection (slide 14)

Risk is highest at diagnosis and at relapse (marrow full of blasts), during immunosuppressive therapy, and with prolonged antibiotic therapy, which breeds resistant organisms and fungal infections.

Neutropenia at home (textbook)

Teach families: hand hygiene, avoid crowds and sick contacts, medical-grade mask in public, ultra-soft toothbrush, safe food handling (wash produce, cook meat well, pasteurized dairy), take temperature if the child feels unwell, and call immediately for a fever. Keep children in school and play as much as safely possible for normal development.

💡 Exam tip
On ATI, the priority for a child on chemo with a fever is infection: assess, cultures, and antibiotics fast. For low platelets: no rectal temps or IM shots, soft toothbrush, no contact sports.
🦠7.11 Immune Deficiency: HIV/AIDS & SCIDPart 3 slides 15–16 · Engage Mod 7
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and AIDS

HIV is a virus that infects and destroys CD4 helper T cells, the “generals” of the immune system. As CD4 counts fall, the child can’t fight infections. AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is the most advanced stage: CD4 below 200 cells/mm³ in older children, or specific opportunistic infections or cancers.

  • Transmission in children: mainly mother-to-child (vertical): across the placenta, during vaginal birth, or through breast milk. Teens: unprotected sex and shared needles. It is not spread by hugging, sharing toys, diaper changes, or saliva.
  • Decreased incidence mother to child (slide): thanks to prenatal screening, maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART), cesarean birth when viral load is high, avoiding breastfeeding in the U.S., and giving the newborn antiretroviral prophylaxis (such as zidovudine).
  • Clinical manifestations = opportunistic infections: infections a healthy immune system would easily handle, such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), oral candidiasis (thrush), recurrent bacterial infections, plus failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, enlarged lymph nodes, developmental delay.
Diagnostic tests (slide)
AgeTestWhy
18 months or youngerPCR (polymerase chain reaction) virologic test that detects the virus itselfThe mother’s antibodies cross the placenta and can stay up to 18 months, so an antibody test would be falsely positive.
Over 18 monthsELISA and Western blot (per the slide)Detect the child’s own antibodies to HIV.
📚 Textbook note (for reference)
Use the slide content (ELISA and Western blot over 18 months) for this course. For reference, the Engage textbook notes that current CDC testing now starts with a fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay (detects antibodies and the p24 antigen, so it catches infection earlier) followed by an antibody differentiation test, and that Western blot is no longer recommended as the confirmatory test. Saliva (rapid) and home tests also exist; a positive rapid test must be confirmed.
Therapeutic management
  • Antiretroviral drugs (ART): a combination taken every day for life. They suppress viral replication but don’t cure. Example: zidovudine (side effects: anemia, bone marrow suppression, nausea). Adherence is everything; missed doses lead to resistance (same time daily, phone alarms, plan for vacations).
  • Prevention of opportunistic infections: PCP prophylaxis (TMP-SMX), routine vaccines (inactivated vaccines; some live vaccines only if CD4 is high enough), annual flu shot.
  • Education to prevent infection: handwashing, standard precautions with blood, safe food, safe sex and condoms for teens; PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis, Truvada) for at-risk HIV-negative teens.
  • Nutrition and exercise: small, frequent, high-calorie, high-protein meals to fight weight loss and diarrhea; normal play and school.
  • Confidentiality and stigma: disclosure is the family’s decision; children with HIV can attend school and play normally.
Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)

SCID is the absence of both humoral (B-cell, antibody) and cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity, often called “bubble boy disease.” It is genetically acquired (often X-linked or autosomal recessive). Babies develop severe, recurrent infections in the first months of life, chronic diarrhea, thrush, and failure to thrive. Diagnosis: many states include it in the newborn screen (TREC test); low lymphocyte counts and absent T cells. Therapeutic management: bone marrow (stem cell) transplant, ideally early; IVIG (immune globulin) for antibodies until then. Nursing considerations: strict protective isolation, meticulous handwashing, no live vaccines, irradiated blood products, family support and genetic counseling.

💡 Exam tip
“Infant under 18 months born to an HIV-positive mother: which test?” → PCR. Antibody tests aren’t reliable until 18 months because of maternal antibodies.
📚

Textbook Extras: More Immune & Blood Disorders

Engage Mod 7 & Mod 11 · Blueprint: “selected disorders of the immune system”
🐝7.12 Allergies & AnaphylaxisEngage Mod 7

An allergy is a type 1 (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. The first exposure to an allergen “sensitizes” the child: B cells make IgE (immunoglobulin E) antibodies that sit on mast cells. On the next exposure, the mast cells burst open and release histamine, causing swelling, itching, and airway narrowing. The most common pediatric allergy is allergic rhinitis; the most severe is anaphylaxis.

  • Common triggers: foods (peanuts, tree nuts, eggs, milk, shellfish), bee stings and insect bites, latex, medications, contrast dye, blood products.
  • Risk factors: family history, eczema (dry skin breaks the barrier), asthma.
  • Localized reaction: sneezing, runny nose, itchy watery eyes, hives.
  • Anaphylaxis (systemic): starts within minutes: stridor, hoarseness, throat tightness, wheezing, widespread hives, facial/lip swelling, flushing, vomiting, hypotension, dizziness, sense of doom.
  • Labs: elevated eosinophils; skin-prick or blood testing to identify allergens.
🚨 Anaphylaxis: epinephrine first
Epinephrine IM in the outer thigh (auto-injector) is the first-line, most important treatment; give it right away, then call 911. Then: airway and oxygen, lay the child flat with legs raised (sitting up if struggling to breathe), IV fluids, and second-line drugs such as diphenhydramine (antihistamine), albuterol (for wheezing), and steroids. Observe for a biphasic (second) reaction for several hours. Expected epinephrine effects: fast heartbeat, shakiness, anxiety.

Teaching: carry two auto-injectors at all times, read food labels, give the school an emergency action plan, wear a medical alert bracelet, avoid the trigger but don’t isolate the child (a child with a nut allergy can go to the party with a safe plan). Early introduction of peanut-containing foods around 4–6 months may help prevent peanut allergy in at-risk infants. Diphenhydramine can cause excitement rather than drowsiness in young children.

💡 Exam tip
Signs of airway involvement (stridor, hoarseness, throat tightness) = epinephrine now. Antihistamines are never a substitute.
🦴7.13 Autoimmune Disorders: JIA & SLEEngage Mod 7
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)

JIA is a group of chronic autoimmune conditions where the immune system inflames the joints (thick, swollen synovial membrane) before age 16, lasting 6 weeks or more. Subtypes include oligoarticular (4 or fewer large joints; highest risk of eye inflammation (uveitis), so regular eye exams), polyarticular (5 or more joints; RF-positive or RF-negative), and systemic (high spiking fevers for 2+ weeks, salmon-colored rash, lymph nodes).

  • Signs: joint swelling, warmth, morning stiffness, limping, growth problems around affected joints.
  • Labs: CBC, ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein) for inflammation, ANA (antinuclear antibody), RF (rheumatoid factor). No single test diagnoses JIA.
  • Treatment: NSAIDs, methotrexate (weekly; give folic acid; avoid live vaccines), biologics such as infliximab, corticosteroids such as prednisone. PT/OT, range-of-motion exercise, swimming, warm baths or showers for morning stiffness, splints at night. Balanced diet with calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin C.
  • Psychosocial: take meds as prescribed (not just when hurting), keep attending school and friends.
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

SLE is a chronic autoimmune disease where antibodies attack the body’s own tissues (skin, joints, kidneys, blood, brain). Most often diagnosed in adolescent females. Hallmark: a malar (butterfly) rash across the cheeks and nose. Other signs: fatigue, fever, joint pain, weight loss, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, Raynaud’s phenomenon, kidney disease (lupus nephritis), and neuropsychiatric signs (headaches, seizures, hearing voices = report).

  • Labs: ANA positive (screen), anti-dsDNA; diagnosis needs several clinical and lab criteria.
  • Treatment: hydroxychloroquine (antimalarial; needs regular eye exams for retinopathy), NSAIDs for joint pain, corticosteroids for flares, belimumab (monoclonal antibody).
  • Teaching: sunscreen SPF 50+, hats, protective clothing; rest and good sleep; infection prevention (higher risk with steroids); never stop steroids abruptly; body-image support for steroid effects (moon face, weight gain).
💡 Exam tip
Butterfly rash + sun sensitivity = SLE → sunscreen teaching. Morning stiffness in a young child = JIA → warm bath and ROM exercises.
🔬7.14 Other Blood Disorders: Thalassemia, Aplastic Anemia, ITP, DIC & LymphomaEngage Mod 11
DisorderWhat goes wrongKey signs and labsTreatment and nursing
Beta-thalassemia major (Cooley anemia)Inherited (autosomal recessive) defect in making the beta chain of hemoglobin → severe anemia; RBCs break down early. Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Asian ancestry.Symptoms appear at 6–24 months: pallor, poor growth, enlarged spleen, bone changes (big forehead/cheekbones). Hgb electrophoresis.Lifelong transfusions → iron overload (heart, liver damage), so chelation therapy (deferoxamine) removes extra iron. Avoid iron supplements. HSCT can cure.
Aplastic anemiaBone marrow stops making all three cell lines (pancytopenia): from drugs, viruses, radiation, toxins, or inherited causes.Anemia (fatigue, pallor), infections (neutropenia), bleeding/bruising (thrombocytopenia). Severe criteria: retic under 1%, ANC under 500, platelets under 20,000. Bone marrow biopsy confirms.HSCT (cure) or immunosuppression: anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) and cyclosporine; eltrombopag to boost platelets. Infection and bleeding precautions.
Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)The immune system destroys platelets, often 1–4 weeks after a viral illness. Usually self-limited in children.Sudden petechiae, bruising, nosebleeds in a child who otherwise looks well; platelets low, other counts normal.Often observation; IVIG or corticosteroids if bleeding. No contact sports, no aspirin/NSAIDs, soft toothbrush.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)A secondary disorder: severe illness (sepsis, burns, trauma, cancer, shock) triggers widespread clotting that uses up platelets and factors → then uncontrolled bleeding.Oozing from IV sites, petechiae, bleeding. Labs: platelets ↓, fibrinogen ↓, PT and PTT prolonged, D-dimer ↑.Treat the cause; replace platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate; heparin in some cases. Gentle oral care, minimize sticks.
Lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin)Cancer of the lymphatic system. Hodgkin has Reed-Sternberg cells (teens/young adults); non-Hodgkin is more aggressive in children.Painless enlarged lymph nodes (neck), fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue; mediastinal mass can compress the airway.Chemotherapy ± radiation; stem cell transplant for relapse. Same infection precautions as leukemia.
💡 Exam tip
Low platelets alone in a well-looking child after a virus = ITP. Low everything = aplastic anemia. Clotting and bleeding in a very sick child = DIC. Transfusion-dependent anemia → watch for iron overload (thalassemia).

Module 8: Genitourinary Disorders in Children

This module follows urine from the kidney to the outside world and what can go wrong on the way: structural problems present at birth (hypospadias, undescended testicles, reflux, obstruction), infections (UTI, pyelonephritis), and kidney inflammation (nephrotic syndrome and glomerulonephritis), plus textbook extras on kidney failure and Wilms tumor.

🎯

Blueprint focus: anatomy and physiology, differentiating congenital vs. acquired disorders, interpreting UA and diagnostic tests, comparing treatments, and family-centered teaching for UTI, VUR, nephrotic syndrome, and AGN.

Lecture 1: Urinary Dysfunction in Children, Part 1

Anatomy · Labs · Structural anomalies · UTI · Engage Mod 8
🫘8.1 The Pediatric GU System: Anatomy, Nephrons & Kidney RiskPart 1 slides 1–5

The genitourinary (GU) system filters waste from the blood and removes it as urine, and it balances fluid, electrolytes, acid-base, and blood pressure. Each kidney contains about a million nephrons. Blood enters the glomerulus, a tiny ball of capillaries that acts like a coffee filter.

A healthy glomerulus lets water and small waste through but blocks large proteins (albumin) and blood cells. That is why protein or blood in the urine signals glomerular damage (nephrotic syndrome and glomerulonephritis).

How children differ (slide 5)
StructureChild vs. adultWhy it matters
KidneyLarge in relation to the abdomen, less protected by fat and ribsProne to injury from trauma
UrethraShorter, especially in girlsBacteria reach the bladder easily → UTIs
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)Slower in infants; reaches adult levels around 2 yearsInfants can’t concentrate urine well or clear drugs quickly → dehydrate and become toxic more easily
Bladder capacityAbout 30 mL in a newborn, increasing with growth (slide: about 270 mL by 1 year); a quick estimate for older kids: (age in years + 2) × 30 mLSmall bladders void often; toilet training usually 2–3 years
Reproductive organsImmature from birth until adolescenceAnomalies found at newborn exam

Normal urine output: about 1–2 mL/kg/hr for infants and children, 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr for adolescents. Weigh diapers: 1 g = 1 mL.

Risk for kidney damage (slide 4)
  • Urinary tract infections in infants: kidneys are still developing and infection spreads upward easily.
  • Delay in starting effective antibacterial treatment: every day of untreated infection raises scarring risk.
  • Anatomic obstruction or congenital anomaly: urine backs up (stasis), bacteria grow.
  • Recurrent episodes of UTI: each kidney infection can leave a scar.
  • Uncircumcised males: bacteria collect under the foreskin; infant boys have more UTIs in the first year.
💡 Exam tip
Kidney scarring can lead to hypertension and chronic kidney disease years later. That is why infant UTIs are treated fast and imaging is done for recurrent or febrile UTIs.
🧪8.2 Labs & Diagnostic StudiesPart 1 slide 6 · Textbook
Urinalysis (UA)
UA findingNormalWhat abnormal suggests
AppearanceClear, pale to amberCloudy, foul-smelling = infection; tea/cola-colored = blood (glomerulonephritis); frothy/foamy = protein (nephrotic syndrome)
ProteinNegative to traceMassive (3+–4+) = nephrotic syndrome; mild-moderate with glomerulonephritis
Blood (RBCs)Negative (2 or fewer RBCs)Glomerulonephritis (with RBC casts), UTI, stones, trauma
WBCs / leukocyte esteraseNegativeInfection (pyuria)
NitritesNegativeBacteria such as E. coli convert nitrates to nitrites → UTI
BacteriaNoneUTI (confirm with culture)
Glucose / ketonesNegativeDiabetes, DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis); ketones also with starvation/vomiting
Specific gravityAbout 1.005–1.030High = concentrated (dehydration); low = dilute
Urine culture and sensitivity (C&S)

The culture grows the organism (results in 24–48 hours) and the sensitivity shows which antibiotics kill it. The most likely organism is Escherichia coli (E. coli), a gut bacterium. Collect the specimen before the first antibiotic dose.

Collection methodUseContamination risk
Clean-catch midstreamToilet-trained children: clean front to back, start voiding, catch the middleModerate
Bag (“wee bag”)Screening UA only in diapered children; never send for cultureHigh (about 50%)
Straight catheterizationPreferred culture method for non-toilet-trained infants/toddlersLow (about 10%)
Suprapubic aspirationNeedle into the bladder (provider, ultrasound-guided)Very low (about 1%)
Blood tests
  • CBC: WBC up with infection; Hgb down in kidney disease (less EPO)
  • GFR (glomerular filtration rate): best overall measure of kidney function
  • BUN (blood urea nitrogen) and creatinine (Cr): rise when kidneys aren’t filtering; creatinine is the more specific kidney marker
  • LFTs (liver function tests), electrolytes (especially potassium), albumin, cholesterol, ASO titer (antistreptolysin O; shows recent strep)
Imaging
  • Renal ultrasound: size, shape, masses, hydronephrosis. Painless, no radiation; a full bladder may be needed.
  • VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram): a catheter fills the bladder with contrast dye and x-rays are taken while the bladder fills and empties. It shows whether urine refluxes into the ureters and kidneys (VUR), which contributes to infections. Prepare the child with age-appropriate explanation, distraction, and possibly sedation; push fluids afterward to flush the dye; mild burning with voiding is expected.
💡 Exam tip
“Which specimen should the nurse send for culture from a 9-month-old?” → catheterized, not a bag specimen.
🧩

Structural Anomalies of the GU Tract

Part 1 slides 7–13 · Engage Mod 8 (CAKUT)
👶8.3 Epispadias, Hypospadias & Bladder ExstrophyPart 1 slides 8–10
⬆️ Epispadias
The urethral opening is on the dorsal (top/upper) surface of the penis, above its normal spot at the tip of the glans. Less common and often occurs with bladder exstrophy.
⬇️ Hypospadias
The urethral opening is on the ventral (underside) of the penis, below the normal spot. Can be anywhere from just under the glans to the scrotum or perineum. Often comes with chordee (downward curve of the penis) and a “dorsal hood” of foreskin.

Memory trick: hypo = below (like hypodermic = under the skin); epi = on top (like epidermis = top layer of skin).

Management (slide 10)
  • Diagnosis is made during the newborn exam: locate the meatus, watch the stream, check for curvature and undescended testes.
  • Should not be circumcised: the foreskin is saved for use in the surgical repair. This is a classic teaching point for parents.
  • Surgical intervention before toilet training, around 6–12 months (textbook: 6–18 months), to reduce body-image stress and allow normal standing urination and future sexual function.
  • After surgery: high fluid intake to keep urine flowing through the stent/catheter; observe for UTI; prophylactic antibiotics; keep the stent or catheter from kinking or being pulled (double diapering is common); pain control; bladder spasms may be treated with oxybutynin; no straddle toys (rocking horses, bikes) for about 3 weeks; tub baths per surgeon.
Bladder exstrophy (textbook)

A serious birth defect in which the bladder develops outside the abdomen, exposed through a gap in the abdominal wall. It can’t store urine. At birth, cover the bladder with clear plastic wrap (not gauze or petroleum gauze, which sticks), keep it moist and clean, and prepare for staged surgical closure. Usually occurs with epispadias.

💡 Exam tip
Parent of a newborn with hypospadias asks about circumcision → “Your baby should not be circumcised now because the foreskin may be needed for the repair.”
🔵8.4 Cryptorchidism & Other Genital ConditionsPart 1 slides 11–13 · Textbook

Cryptorchidism (“hidden testicle”) means at least one testicle has not descended into the scrotum at birth. Testes normally descend during the last months of pregnancy, so:

  • Premature infants have a greater risk; it is one of the most common GU findings (about 1 in 20 male births).
  • Many descend on their own in the first months, but spontaneous descent doesn’t occur after about 1 year.
  • Bilateral in about 1/3 of cases.
  • Left untreated: sterility (the abdomen is too warm for sperm production) and increased risk of testicular cancer. Repair lowers but doesn’t eliminate cancer risk, so teach testicular self-exam in adolescence.
Surgical repair: orchiopexy

The surgery is called an orchiopexy. Surgical correction is done between 6 and 24 months (slide 11), and the surgical care slide notes it is usually done after 12 months. It is minimally invasive and may use a laparoscope to find the testicle, bring it down into the scrotal sac, and anchor it there.

🎯 Purpose of surgery (slide 12)
  • Preserve testicular function (fertility)
  • Provide a normal-appearing scrotum (body image)
  • Make testicular exams easier (cancer detection)
  • Decrease the risk of malignancy
  • A testicular prosthesis can be placed if the testicle is absent or removed

Discharge teaching: similar to hypospadias: give antibiotics/analgesics as prescribed, keep the incision clean, call for signs of infection (fever, redness, drainage, swelling). The child may return to normal diet and activity, avoiding straddle toys and rough play for a short time.

Other genital conditions (textbook)
ConditionWhat it isCare
HydrocelePainless fluid collection in the scrotum; common in newborns; transilluminates (glows with a light)Most resolve by 1–2 years; surgery if it persists or changes size (communicating type can lead to hernia)
PhimosisForeskin too tight to pull back; normal in infants, should loosen by about age 3Never forcibly retract; steroid cream or circumcision if causing problems
ParaphimosisRetracted foreskin stuck behind the glans, swelling itEmergency: reduce the foreskin promptly
Testicular torsion (related knowledge)Testicle twists on its cord, cutting off blood supply: sudden severe pain, swelling, no cremasteric reflexSurgical emergency (within about 6 hours)
💡 Exam tip
Key words: orchiopexy = the surgery; sterility and testicular cancer = the risks; testicular self-exam = the long-term teaching.
🦠

Urinary Tract Infection

Part 1 slides 14–21 · Engage Mod 8
🚽8.5 UTI: Pathophysiology, Signs by Age & Risk FactorsPart 1 slides 15–19 · Lisa case
Case scenario: Lisa (slide 15)

Lisa, 5, has abdominal pain and was sent home after her second accident in 2 days during her first week of kindergarten. The school nurse is concerned about a urinary tract infection. New incontinence in a previously toilet-trained child is a classic UTI clue; don’t assume it’s emotional or developmental until infection is ruled out.

A UTI is an infection anywhere in the urinary tract, most commonly the bladder. Bacteria (usually E. coli from stool) travel up the urethra. Urinary stasis (urine sitting in the bladder) lets bacteria multiply rapidly, because normal voiding flushes them out. UTIs are most common at ages 2–6. In adolescents, ask whether they are sexually active.

Lower UTIUpper UTI
Cystitis (bladder) and urethritis (urethra)Pyelonephritis (kidney) and ureteritis: more serious; can scar the kidney or cause urosepsis
Symptoms change with age (slide 17)
👶 Infants (vague!)
  • Fever (may be the only sign)
  • Irritability
  • Poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhea
  • Poor weight gain (failure to thrive)
  • Foul-smelling urine
🧒 Older children (classic)
  • Fever
  • Poor appetite, vomiting
  • Urinary frequency, hesitancy, urgency
  • Dysuria (painful urination)
  • Hematuria
  • Incontinence or enuresis (new wetting in a toilet-trained child)
  • Abdominal, back, or flank pain
Infant/child with pyelonephritis (slide 18)

High fever, back pain, costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness (pain when tapping the back over the kidneys), nausea and vomiting, chills, and the child appears sick. Young infants with fever and UTI are often hospitalized for IV antibiotics.

Predisposing factors (slide 19)
  • Congenital or acquired obstructions → stasis
  • Phimosis: narrowing of the foreskin in uncircumcised boys traps bacteria
  • Voiding dysfunction: holding urine, incomplete emptying, infrequent voiding
  • Constipation: a full rectum presses on the bladder and stops complete emptying
  • Reflux (VUR): urine washes back up toward the kidneys
  • Sexually active teens
  • Anatomic differences in young girls: a short urethra and its close proximity to the perirectal area (anus), so stool bacteria are close by. Also: wiping back to front, bubble baths, tight clothing, diapers.
💡 Exam tip
Why girls get more UTIs (after the first year): short urethra close to the anus. In the first year, uncircumcised boys have more.
💊8.6 UTI Management & EducationPart 1 slides 20–21 · Textbook
Nursing management (slide 20)
  • Does the child need to be hospitalized? Depends on uncomplicated vs. complicated infection and age: young infants (especially under 2 months), toxic-appearing children, those vomiting and unable to keep down oral meds, or with pyelonephritis/urosepsis need IV therapy.
  • Antibiotic therapy: oral or IV? Common choices: 1st, 2nd, or 3rd generation cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefdinir, ceftriaxone IV), nitrofurantoin (bladder infections only; doesn’t reach the kidney), amoxicillin-clavulanate, TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; not under 2 months).
  • Duration: 3–5 days for simple cystitis; about 10 days for febrile children (7–14 days).
  • Increased fluid intake to flush bacteria.
  • Acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain and fever.
  • Warm compresses; void in a warm sitz or tub bath if urination burns. Phenazopyridine may be used in older children for burning (turns urine bright orange).
  • Symptoms should improve in 24–48 hours; call if not.
Education (slide 21)
✅ Prevention teaching
  • Take the full course of antibiotics, even when better
  • Hygiene: wipe from front to back
  • Avoid bubble baths (irritate the urethra)
  • Avoid “holding” urine; void every 3–4 hours and remind kids to take bathroom breaks from play
  • Plenty of fluids (water)
  • Correct constipation: fiber, fluids
  • Cotton underwear; avoid tight-fitting clothing
  • Void after intercourse for sexually active adolescent females
📞 Follow-up
  • Recurrent or febrile UTIs → ultrasound ± VCUG to look for VUR or obstruction
  • Cranberry juice has limited evidence in children
  • Measure liquid antibiotics with an oral syringe, not a household spoon
💡 Exam tip
An ATI favorite: a parent says “I’ll stop the antibiotic when the fever is gone” → needs more teaching. Another: bubble baths and wiping back to front increase risk.
🔁

Lecture 2: Urinary Dysfunction, Part 2

Obstructive uropathy · VUR · Nephrotic syndrome · Glomerulonephritis
↩️8.7 Obstructive Uropathy, Vesicoureteral Reflux & VCUGPart 2 slides 2–8
Obstructive uropathy

A structural or functional blockage at any level of the upper or lower urinary tract. Urine backs up above the obstruction and can cause hydronephrosis (a swollen, fluid-filled kidney). Often found on prenatal ultrasound. Early diagnosis and surgical correction are essential to preserve kidney function. Clues in a newborn: no void in the first 24 hours, weak stream, palpable bladder or kidney, recurrent UTIs.

Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR)

Normally a one-way “valve” where the ureter enters the bladder stops urine from going back up. In VUR, urine flows from the bladder back up into the ureters during voiding. This leftover urine (stasis) breeds bacteria, and if the urine is infected the child is at risk for pyelonephritis. Untreated, it can cause kidney scarring, hypertension (HTN), and chronic kidney disease.

Grade (per slide)Treatment
Grades 1–2 (mild)Often resolve on their own as the child grows; monitor
Grades 3–4Prophylactic (daily low-dose) antibiotics and periodic VCUG checks
Grades 4–5 with frequent UTIsSurgery (ureteral reimplantation, or endoscopic injection) to preserve kidney function
VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram) (slide 7)

Indications: determine the grade of reflux, evaluate hydronephrosis or renal scarring, and investigate recurrent febrile UTIs. How it’s done: the bladder is catheterized and contrast is instilled until the bladder is full; images of the full bladder, the ureter-bladder junction, the kidneys, and the urethra are taken, including while the child voids. Nursing: explain with dolls or pictures, have the parent present, distraction; afterward encourage fluids and watch for UTI signs.

Education, prevention, and post-op care (slide 8)
🛡️ Prevent infections
  • Empty the bladder completely; double-voiding (void, wait, void again)
  • Perianal and toileting hygiene
  • Prophylactic antibiotics if prescribed
  • Follow up on urine cultures and VCUGs
  • Treat constipation
🏥 Postoperative care
  • Vital signs; daily weight
  • Fluids to increase urine output; strict I&O
  • Monitor urine output from the Foley catheter or stents: bloody urine should clear within 2–3 days
  • Avoid manipulating the catheter or stent to reduce bladder spasms
  • Analgesics (and antispasmodics)
💡 Exam tip
Pink-tinged urine for the first 2–3 days after reimplant surgery is expected; bright red or clots after that, or no output from a catheter = notify the provider.
🎈8.8 Nephrotic SyndromePart 2 slides 9–16
Case scenario (slide 9)

A mother brings her 4-year-old boy in for facial edema and swollen feet. Why does the provider want a urine specimen? Because puffiness in a young child points to the kidneys losing protein: the urine dipstick will show massive proteinuria.

Pathophysiology

Types are congenital, primary, and secondary. The most common primary type in children is minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS), usually ages 2–7, more common in boys. Normally the glomerular membrane is impermeable to large proteins. In nephrotic syndrome it becomes leaky, so protein, especially albumin, pours into the urine (proteinuria). Serum albumin drops, so the blood loses the protein “sponge” (oncotic pressure) that holds water inside the vessels. Fluid shifts from the plasma into the interstitial spaces → edema. The liver responds by making more lipoproteins → hyperlipidemia.

Clinical manifestations (slide 11)
  • Weight gain from fluid
  • Edema: periorbital (puffy eyes, worst in the morning), anasarca (generalized total-body edema), ascites (fluid in the abdomen), pretibial (shins), scrotal/labial
  • Blood pressure is usually normal (normotensive) or low; hypertension is uncommon (a key difference from glomerulonephritis)
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Decreased urine output, frothy (foamy) urine
  • Fatigue, lethargy, irritability
  • Anorexia, diarrhea (gut wall edema)
Diagnostic evaluation (slide 12)
TestFinding
UrinalysisMassive proteinuria (3+ or more), possibly a few RBCs, fatty casts
Serum albuminVery low (often under 2.5 g/dL)
Cholesterol/lipidsHigh
BUN and creatinineUsually normal in MCNS
ElectrolytesSodium may be low (dilutional)
Treatment (slide 14)
  • May be hospitalized for diagnosis and treatment
  • Prednisone 2 mg/kg per day until remission (protein-free urine for 3 days), usually 4–6 weeks, then tapered slowly (never stopped suddenly)
  • Diuretics (furosemide), sometimes with IV albumin, for severe edema
  • Oral antibiotics: these children are prone to infection (especially peritonitis) from steroids and lost antibodies
  • Live vaccines are contraindicated during high-dose steroids (MMR, varicella); give pneumococcal and yearly flu vaccines
  • Strict I&O, daily weights (same scale, same time), abdominal girth, urine dipstick for protein
  • Prevent skin breakdown: turn often, support and elevate edematous areas, pillows between knees, cotton underwear and scrotal support, keep skin folds clean and dry
  • Prevent infection: handwashing, private room away from sick children, monitor temperature, teach family
  • Diet: protein-rich snacks (normal-to-high protein), low sodium (“no added salt”), fluid restriction only with severe edema; potassium per labs (diuretics can lower it)
Education (slide 15)

Teach about the disease and relapse (common), nutrition, rest, infection control, follow-up care (BP, weights, urine dipstick at home to catch relapse early), and prednisone adverse effects: hirsutism (extra hair), weight gain and moon face, mood changes, hypertension, hyperglycemia, plus infection risk and slowed growth. Provide emotional support for body image, especially for school-age children and teens.

💡 Exam tip
Nephrotic = “Protein out, fluid in”: massive proteinuria, low albumin, high lipids, generalized edema, usually normal BP, preschool age, treated with steroids.
🫖8.9 Acute Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis (APSGN)Part 2 slides 17–22

APSGN is an inflammation of the glomeruli that follows a streptococcal infection of the throat (strep throat/URI, upper respiratory infection) or skin (impetigo). The body makes antibodies against group A beta-hemolytic strep; antigen-antibody complexes get deposited in the glomerulus and cause inflammation. The inflamed glomeruli filter poorly, so the body retains sodium and water (edema, hypertension) and lets RBCs leak into the urine.

  • Latent period of 10–14 days after the strep infection (throat about 1–2 weeks; skin up to 3–6 weeks)
  • Primarily affects early school-age children; peak age 7; boys twice as often
  • Usually self-limited with full recovery
Clinical manifestations (slide 19)
  • Ill appearance, lethargy, anorexia
  • Edema, especially periorbital/facial in the morning (milder than nephrotic)
  • Decreased urine output (oliguria)
  • Smoky, tea-, or cola-colored urine (hematuria)
  • Mild to severely elevated blood pressure: watch for hypertensive encephalopathy (headache, blurred vision, vomiting, seizures)
  • Headache, abdominal discomfort, dysuria

Labs: UA with hematuria (RBC casts) and mild-moderate proteinuria; elevated BUN/creatinine; positive ASO titer (proof of recent strep); low complement (C3).

Treatment (slide 20)
  • Supportive care and medical management while the kidneys heal
  • Fluid and electrolyte management: restrict fluids and sodium, potassium restriction if oliguric; strict I&O and daily weights
  • Antihypertensive therapy (for example, an ACE inhibitor such as captopril); check BP frequently
  • Antibiotic therapy only if strep infection is still present (to clear it; doesn’t reverse the kidney inflammation)
  • Diuretics (furosemide) for edema and BP
  • Adequate rest: quiet activities while BP and hematuria are high
  • Maintain skin integrity due to edema
  • Maintain nutrition (small appealing meals, no added salt)
  • Relieve anxiety; seizure precautions if BP is very high
Education (slide 21)

Nutritional management (low salt), teach the family to monitor BP and daily weights, how to give medications and watch for side effects, infection control, and encourage the child to talk about body image. Prevention: treat strep infections promptly and completely.

Nephrotic syndrome vs. APSGN
Nephrotic syndromeAPSGN
CauseUsually unknown (minimal change)Strep infection 10–14 days earlier
Age2–7 yearsEarly school age (peak 7)
UrineMassive protein, frothyHematuria (tea/cola), mild protein
EdemaSevere, generalized (anasarca)Mild, periorbital
Blood pressureNormal or lowHigh
SerumVery low albumin, high lipidsHigh BUN/Cr, +ASO titer, low C3
Main treatmentPrednisoneSupportive: antihypertensives, diuretics, Na/fluid restriction

Practice question from slide 22: Which child is at risk for glomerulonephritis? The 3-year-old who had impetigo one week ago (impetigo is a strep skin infection). And slide 23: females have increased UTI risk due to the short urethra.

💡 Exam tip
APSGN = “Strep, then cola and pressure”. Priority assessment: blood pressure (encephalopathy risk) and daily weight/I&O.
📚

Textbook Extras: Kidney Failure & Wilms Tumor

Engage Mod 8
⚠️8.10 Acute Kidney Injury, Chronic Kidney Disease & Wilms TumorEngage Mod 8
Acute kidney injury (AKI)Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
OnsetSudden (hours to days); often reversibleSlow (months to years); progressive and not reversible
CausesPrerenal (poor blood flow: dehydration, shock, hemorrhage, the most common in children), intrarenal (kidney damage: APSGN, nephrotoxic drugs, HUS), postrenal (obstruction)Congenital anomalies (CAKUT, about 60%), glomerular disease, reflux scarring
First signSudden drop in urine output (oliguria)Fatigue, poor growth, pallor (anemia), hypertension, bone problems, enuresis
TreatmentTreat the cause; strict fluid balance; treat hyperkalemia; dialysis if neededACE inhibitors, epoetin (for anemia), vitamin D and phosphate binders (bones), growth hormone, diet; dialysis and transplant
🚨 Hyperkalemia: the deadly lab
When kidneys fail, potassium builds up and can cause dangerous cardiac dysrhythmias (peaked T waves). Early signs: weakness, nausea, chest discomfort. Treatment: put the child on a cardiac monitor; IV calcium gluconate protects the heart, insulin with glucose pushes potassium into cells, sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate/Kionex) removes it through the gut, dialysis if severe. Limit high-potassium foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes, tomatoes).
Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma)

The most common kidney cancer in children, usually under age 5. Parents often notice a firm, painless abdominal mass on one side while bathing or dressing the child; there may be hypertension or hematuria. Linked with some syndromes (WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann). Treatment: surgery to remove the kidney (nephrectomy), chemo, ± radiation; prognosis is very good.

🚫 Do NOT palpate the abdomen
Before surgery, post a sign on the bed: “Do not palpate abdomen.” Pressing on the tumor can rupture its capsule and spread cancer cells. Handle and bathe the child gently.
💡 Exam tip
Wilms tumor = don’t touch the belly. AKI = watch the potassium and urine output.

Module 9: Neuromuscular, Musculoskeletal & Neurological Disorders

Two lectures in one tab. Neuro: assessing the brain, recognizing rising pressure in the skull, head injuries, meningitis, seizures, hydrocephalus, spina bifida, and brain tumors. Neuromuscular and musculoskeletal: what immobility does to the body, fractures and casts, hip dysplasia, clubfoot, spinal curves, brittle bone disease, cerebral palsy, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

🎯

Blueprint focus: recognizing subtle neuro and musculoskeletal changes, interpreting assessments and diagnostics, safety, positioning, mobility support, and collaboration with PT/OT and rehabilitation.
