Lecture 1: Neurological System

Neuro assessment · ICP · TBI · Meningitis · Seizures · Hydrocephalus · Spina bifida · Tumors · Engage Mod 10
🔦9.1 The Pediatric Neuro Assessment & Glasgow Coma ScaleNeuro slides 2–3

A neuro assessment checks how well the brain and nerves are working: level of consciousness (LOC), pupils, movement and strength, reflexes, and vital signs. The most important rule on the slide: always compare the current assessment to the child’s own baseline, including pregnancy and delivery history. A change from baseline matters more than any single number.

👶 The “under 2” challenge
Babies can’t follow commands or answer questions, so assessment relies on primitive reflexes (Moro, rooting, grasp), the cry (strong vs. weak or high-pitched), smiling, tracking, consolability, and interaction with parents. Also check the anterior fontanel (soft spot): flat and soft is normal; bulging/tense = increased pressure; sunken = dehydration. Measure head circumference.
💓 Vital sign variability
In neuro problems the pulse can be slow or fast, breathing may become slow or shallow, and BP is highly variable. Trend them over time.
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
CategoryPointsChild 2 years and olderUnder 2 years (modified verbal)
Eye opening4 → 1Spontaneously 4 · to speech 3 · to pain 2 · none 1Same
Best verbal5 → 1Oriented 5 · confused 4 · inappropriate words 3 · incomprehensible sounds 2 · none 1Smiles, listens, follows 5 · cries but consolable 4 · inappropriate persistent cry 3 · agitated, restless 2 · no response 1
Best motor6 → 1Obeys commands 6 · localizes pain 5 · withdraws 4 · abnormal flexion (decorticate) 3 · extension (decerebrate) 2 · none 1Spontaneous movement in place of obeying

Maximum score is 15 (fully awake); the lowest is 3. A score of 8 or lower indicates coma and usually means the child can’t protect their airway (“8 = intubate”). A drop of 2 or more points is significant. Pupils: check size (mm) and reaction: ++ brisk, + sluggish, – no reaction, C eye closed by swelling. Also check hand grip equality and muscle tone (normal, spastic, flaccid, arching, decorticate, decerebrate).

💡 Exam tip
The earliest and most sensitive sign of neurologic change is a change in LOC (irritability, lethargy, not recognizing parents), before pupils or vital signs change.
📈9.2 Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP)Neuro slide 5

The skull is a closed box holding brain, blood, and CSF (cerebrospinal fluid). If any of these increases (swelling, bleeding, tumor, extra CSF), pressure rises and squeezes the brain. Infants have open sutures and fontanels, so the head can expand a little, which is why their signs differ.

Early signs: infants and young children
  • Tense, bulging anterior fontanel
  • High-pitched cry
  • Increasing head circumference, separated sutures
  • Setting-sun sign (eyes deviated downward with white sclera showing above the iris)
  • Irritability and poor feeding, distended scalp veins
Early signs: older children
  • Projectile vomiting, often in the morning without nausea
  • Headache, worse lying down or on waking
  • Diplopia (double vision) or blurred vision
  • Personality and cognitive changes, falling school performance
  • Seizures
🚨 Late signs: life-threatening red flags
  • Bradycardia (with high BP and irregular breathing this is Cushing triad: impending brain herniation)
  • Cheyne-Stokes respirations (cycles of deep breathing then apnea)
  • Altered pupil size and reactivity (fixed and dilated)
  • Extension or flexion posturing (decerebrate/decorticate)
  • Decreased response to painful stimuli
  • Papilledema (swollen optic disc)
  • Progressing to coma
Nursing care (slide)
  • Keep the head and neck in neutral alignment (no flexion or turning) so blood drains out of the brain; HOB elevated about 30°.
  • Monitor hydration and prevent weight loss: fluids are often carefully restricted; daily weights and I&O.
  • Monitor for SIADH or DI: brain injury can disturb ADH (antidiuretic hormone). SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH) = too much ADH → low urine output, fluid retention, low sodium (seizure risk). DI (diabetes insipidus) = too little ADH → huge amounts of dilute urine, dehydration, high sodium.
  • Avoid things that spike ICP: crying, coughing, straining (stool softeners), suctioning longer than needed, clustering too many procedures; quiet, dim room; seizure precautions.
💡 Exam tip
Infant + bulging fontanel + high-pitched cry = increased ICP. Bradycardia and posturing are late; report immediately.
⛑️9.3 Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) & Abusive Head TraumaNeuro slide 6 · Textbook

A TBI is an injury to the brain from a blow to the head or neck. Head injury is the most common cause of death and disability in children. Common causes: falls (young children), sports and bikes (school-age), motor vehicle crashes (teens), and abuse (infants). Children are vulnerable because their heads are large and heavy for their bodies and neck muscles are weak.

TypeWhat happensKey points
Concussion (mild)The brain bounces or twists inside the skull from a direct or indirect hit (coup-contrecoup: injury where it hit and on the opposite side). Chemical changes but typically no permanent tissue damage.Headache (most common), confusion, dizziness, nausea, memory loss, sensitivity to light and noise, sleep changes. Treatment: cognitive and physical rest for 24–48 hours (no screens, schoolwork, reading, sports), then a gradual stepwise return; no return to play the same day.
Contusion and lacerationRuptured blood vessels cause bleeding (bruising) or tearing of brain tissue, typically in the temporal or frontal lobes.Loss of consciousness, vomiting, seizures, speech/vision problems. Can cause permanent neurological impairment.
Subdural hematomaVenous rupture: blood pools between the dura mater and the brain.Most common hematoma; often more diffuse; may develop more slowly. Classic in abusive head trauma.
Epidural hematomaArterial rupture (often middle meningeal artery with a skull fracture): blood pools between the skull and the dura.Expands rapidly due to arterial pressure. Classic pattern: brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval (seems fine), then rapid decline. Surgical emergency.
👶 Abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome)
Violent shaking (with or without impact) of an infant or young child tears bridging veins (subdural hematoma) and causes retinal hemorrhages, brain swelling, and often rib or long-bone fractures. Signs can be subtle: irritability, vomiting without fever, poor feeding, lethargy, seizures, apnea. It leads to severe neurological, internal organ, and musculoskeletal injuries and is often fatal or results in lifelong disability. Nurses are mandated reporters. Teach parents that crying is normal and it’s OK to put the baby down safely and walk away.
Nursing care
  • Assess airway, breathing, circulation, then spine (assume a neck injury until cleared), then neuro (GCS, pupils, LOC).
  • Imaging (CT/MRI) for loss of consciousness, worsening symptoms, or suspected bleeding; a concussion alone doesn’t require imaging.
  • Home observation after a mild head injury: wake the child as directed and return immediately for repeated vomiting, worsening headache, unequal pupils, confusion, unusual sleepiness, seizures, weakness, clear fluid from the nose or ears (CSF leak; tests positive for glucose).
  • Treat pain with acetaminophen; avoid NSAIDs if bleeding is suspected (the slide/textbook allow OTC NSAIDs for a simple concussion headache once bleeding is ruled out).
  • Prevention: helmets, car seats, window guards, safe play.
💡 Exam tip
“Epidural = arterial = rapid”; “Subdural = venous = most common, slower.” After a concussion: rest 24–48 hours, then gradual return.
🧪9.4 Meningitis: Pathophysiology, Signs & DiagnosisNeuro slide 7 · Textbook

Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, the protective layers covering the brain and spinal cord, caused by bacteria or viruses in the CSF. Bacterial (septic) meningitis is a medical emergency (common organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, group B strep and E. coli in newborns; Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) is now rare thanks to vaccines). Viral (aseptic) meningitis is more common and usually milder and self-limited.

AgeHow it presents
NewbornsVague: poor tone (floppy), weak cry, refusing to feed, temperature instability (often low), lethargy, apnea. Bulging fontanel is a late sign.
3 months–2 yearsFever, seizures, high-pitched cry, bulging fontanel, irritability that gets worse when held (paradoxical irritability), poor feeding, vomiting
2 years–adolescenceFever, headache, photophobia, vomiting, altered LOC, nuchal rigidity (stiff neck), positive Brudzinski sign (bending the neck makes the hips and knees flex), positive Kernig sign (pain/resistance when straightening the leg with the hip flexed)
Lumbar puncture (LP): CSF analysis
CSF metricBacterial (septic)Viral (aseptic)
ColorCloudyClear
WBC countElevated (neutrophils)Slightly elevated (lymphocytes)
ProteinElevatedNormal to slightly elevated
GlucoseDecreased (bacteria eat the sugar)Normal
Gram stainPositiveNegative

LP positioning: older child side-lying with knees to chest and chin tucked (“shrimp”), or sitting and leaning forward; infants are held sitting up curled forward or side-lying. Watch the infant’s breathing and SpO₂ during the hold. Afterward, lie flat as ordered and check the site. LP is delayed if there are signs of very high ICP. Blood cultures and CSF should be obtained before antibiotics when possible, but antibiotics must not be delayed.

💡 Exam tip
Bacterial CSF = cloudy, high protein, low glucose. Viral = clear with normal glucose. Newborns don’t show neck stiffness; look for poor feeding and a weak cry.
🛡️9.5 Meningitis Interventions & EncephalitisNeuro slide 8 · Textbook
🚨 Immediate action required
The presence of petechiae or a purpuric (purple, non-blanching) rash suggests meningococcemia (Neisseria meningitidis in the blood), which can progress to shock and DIC within hours. Notify the provider immediately; it requires immediate medical attention.
😷 Isolation
  • Start droplet precautions immediately upon suspicion (don’t wait for results)
  • Private room
  • Maintain respiratory isolation for at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics
  • Close contacts of meningococcal disease get prophylactic antibiotics (rifampin)
🌙 Environment & care
  • Decrease stimuli: quiet room, dim lighting, cool temperature (photophobia, seizure risk)
  • Position without a pillow, HOB slightly elevated (side-lying with neck support is often most comfortable); avoid neck flexion
  • NPO if decreased LOC (aspiration risk)
  • Restrict fluids until ICP normalizes to prevent cerebral edema (watch for SIADH)
  • Seizure precautions; neuro checks; measure head circumference in infants; I&O
  • Treat fever and pain (acetaminophen)
💊 Medications
  • IV antibiotics as soon as possible for bacterial meningitis, given for up to 21 days (usually 7–21 depending on the organism). Complete the entire course.
  • Dexamethasone (corticosteroid) given with or just before the first antibiotic dose helps with initial ICP and inflammation; most effective for Hib meningitis (reduces hearing loss); not indicated for viral meningitis.
  • Viral meningitis: supportive care (rest, fluids, analgesics); acyclovir if herpes is suspected.

Complications to watch for: hearing loss (the most common; arrange a hearing test before discharge), seizures, hydrocephalus, SIADH, developmental delay, and in meningococcemia, shock, DIC, and limb loss. Prevention: Hib, pneumococcal (PCV), and meningococcal vaccines (MenACWY for preteens, booster at 16).

Encephalitis (textbook)

Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain tissue itself, usually from a virus (enteroviruses, herpes simplex, mosquito- or tick-borne viruses such as West Nile). Signs: fever, headache, confusion, behavior changes, hallucinations, seizures, photophobia, and decreased LOC. Diagnosed by LP (CSF protein may be up) and MRI/EEG. Treatment is supportive (airway, fluids, anticonvulsants, ICP control) plus IV acyclovir for herpes. Long-term effects can include seizures, memory and speech problems. Prevent with vaccines (MMR), insect repellent, and avoiding mosquito/tick bites.

💡 Exam tip
First nursing action for suspected bacterial meningitis: droplet precautions (then antibiotics ASAP). Rash that doesn’t blanch = meningococcemia, emergency.
⚡9.6 Febrile Seizures & Epilepsy ClassificationsNeuro slide 9 · Textbook

A seizure is a sudden burst of uncontrolled electrical activity in the brain that changes movement, behavior, sensation, or awareness.

Febrile seizures
  • Triggered by a sudden rise in body temperature above 38°C (100.4°F), typically from a viral illness (cold, flu, roseola). It’s the speed of the rise, not just how high it goes.
  • Most common in children under 5 (6 months–5 years), peak incidence at 2 years; family history raises risk; about 1 in 25 children have one.
  • Simple febrile: generalized (affects the whole body), short (under 15 minutes), only once in 24 hours. Complex febrile: focal (one part of the body), prolonged (over 15 minutes), or repeats within 24 hours; slightly higher epilepsy risk.
  • Treatment: fever management with acetaminophen or ibuprofen for comfort (antipyretics do not prevent recurrence), find and treat the cause. LP if meningitis is possible.
  • Prognosis: simple febrile seizures do not typically cause long-term developmental delays or learning effects; about a third recur.
  • Teach parents: stay calm, place the child on their side on a safe surface, time it, nothing in the mouth, don’t put the child in a cool bath; call 911 if it lasts more than 5 minutes, breathing is affected, or it’s the first seizure.
Epilepsy

Epilepsy is defined as two or more unprovoked seizures occurring at least 24 hours apart (unprovoked = no fever, low sugar, injury, or other trigger). About 1–2% of U.S. children have it; many outgrow it.

ClassificationWhere it startsWhat it looks like
GeneralizedBoth sides of the brain at once; consciousness is lostTonic-clonic (stiffening, then rhythmic jerking; postictal sleepiness), myoclonic (quick muscle jerks), atonic (sudden loss of tone, “drop attacks,” needs a helmet), absence (brief staring spells, a few seconds, often mistaken for daydreaming)
FocalOne specific side or area of the brainMay start with an aura. Motor (jerking of one limb) or non-motor: automatisms (lip smacking, picking at clothes), altered consciousness. Can spread to become generalized.
CombinedBoth generalized and focal seizuresOften seen in developmental epileptic syndromes such as Dravet syndrome (starts in infancy, often with fever)
UnknownOrigin of the discharge unknownManifestations vary widely; may include epileptic spasms
💡 Exam tip
“Two or more unprovoked, 24 hours apart” = epilepsy. Febrile seizure teaching: fever reducers are for comfort, not prevention.
🛟9.7 Epilepsy Management & Seizure SafetyNeuro slide 10 · Textbook
Acute nursing care: safety first (slide)
  • Pad the crib or bed rails; keep the bed low, suction and oxygen at the bedside
  • Stay with the child; move them to a flat, safe surface and clear the area
  • Promote a patent airway: turn on the side so saliva drains, loosen clothing; never put anything in the mouth
  • Do not interrupt the child or restrain movements
  • Record seizure activity: start time, duration, what it looked like, body parts involved, eyes, breathing, color, incontinence, and the postictal state
  • Administer Diastat (rectal diazepam) as needed (or intranasal midazolam) for a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more; seizures over 5 minutes or back-to-back without recovery = status epilepticus, an emergency (IV lorazepam in the hospital)
  • After the seizure: side-lying (recovery) position, check vitals and neuro status, let the child rest, reorient
Diagnostics (slide)
  • Electroencephalogram (EEG): electrodes on the scalp record brain waves and detect epileptiform discharges. Prep: clean hair with no oils; sometimes sleep-deprived; usually hold caffeine.
  • MRI: looks for structural brain defects or tumors.
Long-term therapies (slide)
TherapyDetails
Pharmacological: anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs)Monitor serum drug levels closely. Never stop suddenly (rebound seizures/status epilepticus). Examples: phenytoin (gum overgrowth → good dental care; narrow therapeutic range 10–20 mcg/mL), carbamazepine (blood counts, hyponatremia, no grapefruit), valproate (liver toxicity, pancreatitis, low platelets; risky under age 2), levetiracetam (mood/behavior changes). AEDs can increase suicidal thoughts and many cause birth defects (teach teens contraception).
Dietary: ketogenic or modified Atkins dietHigh fat, low carbohydrate, moderate protein; the body burns fat (ketones), which reduces seizures. Managed by a dietitian; watch for kidney stones, constipation, low sugar.
Surgical/deviceVagus nerve stimulator (VNS) or focal brain surgery for seizures that don’t respond to medication (see note below).
📝 Note: VNS placement (your course vs. common practice)
For this course, use the course wording: both your slide (“Implant a Vagus Nerve Stimulator (VNS) in the upper left cheek”) and your Engage textbook (“implanted under the skin on the left side of the upper cheek”) say upper left cheek. The device sends regular electrical pulses through the left vagus nerve to reduce and shorten seizures; the family can swipe a magnet over it at the start of a seizure for an extra pulse. For reference, in common practice the generator is placed under the skin of the upper left chest, below the collarbone, with a wire tunneled to the left vagus nerve in the neck.
Living with epilepsy

Seizure action plan for school; supervised swimming and showers instead of baths; helmets for bikes (and for atonic seizures); medical alert ID; adequate sleep and stress management; avoid known triggers (flashing lights for some); driving only after seizure-free for the time required by state law. Encourage normal school and social life.

💡 Exam tip
During a seizure the priorities are safety and airway (side-lying, nothing in the mouth, don’t restrain, time it). The most important AED teaching is don’t stop it suddenly.
💧9.8 Hydrocephalus & the VP ShuntNeuro slides 11–12 · Textbook

Hydrocephalus (“water on the brain”) is an increased accumulation of CSF in the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces, from impaired absorption (most common), excessive production, or obstructed circulation. The ventricles enlarge and ICP rises. It is often linked with myelomeningocele (spina bifida), prematurity with bleeding in the brain, infection, or tumors.

👶 Infant presentation
  • Rapidly increasing head circumference (measure daily at the widest point)
  • Tense, bulging fontanels, separated sutures
  • Prominent scalp veins
  • Downward-deviated eyes (“sunset sign”)
  • High-pitched cry and irritability
  • Poor muscle tone, poor feeding, vomiting
🧒 Toddler and older child
  • Severe headaches (worse in the morning)
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Vision problems (diplopia or crossed eyes)
  • Balance and gait issues
  • Developmental delays
  • Subtle decline in school performance
Primary treatment: the VP shunt

A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is surgically placed to continuously drain excess CSF from the brain’s ventricle to the abdominal (peritoneal) cavity, where it is absorbed. A one-way valve controls flow. Alternative: endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV), which makes a small opening so CSF can bypass a blockage without a shunt.

Post-operative nursing care (slide)
  • Neurologic assessment: watch for pupil dilation on the same side as the pressure (it means the oculomotor nerve, cranial nerve III, is being compressed); LOC, fontanel, head circumference.
  • Vital signs: watch for BP variability from brainstem hypoxia.
  • Abdominal assessment: distention or constipation (risk of CSF peritonitis or postoperative ileus); bowel sounds.
  • Positioning: usually flat at first and on the non-operative side (not on the valve), then HOB raised gradually per order; raising too fast can drain CSF too quickly. Don’t pump the shunt unless ordered.
  • Pain control, I&O, monitor the incision for leaking CSF.
⚠️ Major complications
Malfunction: often from mechanical obstruction (tissue or exudate in the ventricle) or the distal end pulling out as the child grows. Signs = increased ICP, but they can be subtle: behavior changes, intermittent headaches, vomiting, sleepiness, declining school performance, and in infants a growing head or bulging fontanel. Shunts often need revisions as children grow.
Infection: can occur any time, but greatest risk is within the first month after placement: fever, redness along the tubing, poor feeding, irritability, decreased LOC, abdominal pain. Treated with IV antibiotics, sometimes shunt removal.

Family teaching: signs of shunt malfunction and infection (call immediately), avoid contact sports or use protective gear per the neurosurgeon, medical alert ID, keep follow-up appointments.

💡 Exam tip
The first sign of shunt malfunction in an older child is often subtle: headache, irritability, lethargy, a drop in grades, not a dramatic change.
🎗️9.9 Spina Bifida: Neural Tube DefectsNeuro slide 13 · Textbook

Spina bifida is a neural tube defect: incomplete closure of the spinal cord and its bony covering during the 2nd to 6th week of gestation (often before a person knows they’re pregnant). Most common in the lumbar/sacral spine.

TypeWhat’s involvedEffects
Spina bifida occulta (“hidden”)An opening in the vertebrae without protrusion; cord and meninges stay insideOften seen only as a hairy patch, dimple, birthmark, or fatty lump on the lower back. Rarely causes problems.
MeningoceleA sac containing spinal fluid and meninges, but no nervesUsually minor complications and normal motor function after surgical closure.
MyelomeningoceleThe most severe form. Sac contains meninges, spinal fluid, and nerves (spinal cord)Varying neurological deficits, paralysis below the defect, loss of sensation, bowel and bladder incontinence (neurogenic bladder), clubfoot and hip problems. Often linked with hydrocephalus (about 80–90% need a shunt) and Chiari II malformation.
Prevention and screening
  • 400 mcg of folic acid daily for all females of childbearing age, starting before conception (higher doses, 4,000 mcg, if a previous child had a neural tube defect). Foods: fortified cereals, leafy greens, citrus, legumes.
  • Prenatal screening: maternal alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) blood test (elevated = possible open neural tube defect) and ultrasound in the second trimester. Fetal surgery is an option in some centers.
  • Risk factors: low folate, maternal diabetes or obesity, some anti-seizure drugs (valproate), hyperthermia (hot tubs) in early pregnancy.
Initial postnatal care (myelomeningocele)
  • Prevent infection and physically protect the sac before surgery: cover with a sterile, moist, nonadherent dressing (sterile saline), changed often; nothing touches it.
  • Position prone (on the belly) or side-lying with hips slightly flexed; no diaper over the sac; keep stool away (a barrier/drape below the sac).
  • Watch the sac for leaking or tears and for infection; measure head circumference daily and watch for increased ICP (hydrocephalus).
  • Early surgical closure within 12–72 hours after birth to prevent infection (meningitis) and further nerve damage.
  • Latex precautions from birth: these children develop latex allergy from repeated catheterizations and surgeries.
Long-term care

Watch for tethered cord syndrome as the child grows (the cord is stuck and stretches: new back pain, worsening walking, changes in bladder or bowel control, scoliosis). Clean intermittent catheterization (children can learn self-cath in the early school years), bowel program, skin checks for pressure injuries (no sensation), braces/wheelchair, PT/OT, shunt monitoring, encourage independence and self-care.

💡 Exam tip
Newborn with myelomeningocele: prone position + sterile moist saline dressing + latex-free. Mother-to-be teaching: 400 mcg folic acid daily.
🧠9.10 Brain TumorsNeuro slide 14 · Textbook

Brain tumors are the most common solid tumor in children, about 25% of all childhood cancers (second only to leukemia overall). Most childhood brain tumors are in the back of the brain (posterior fossa: cerebellum and brainstem), so balance problems are common.

Signs of increased ICP (slide)
  • Severe morning headaches (pressure builds lying down overnight)
  • Nausea and vomiting immediately upon awakening, often without nausea first, and the headache may feel better after vomiting
  • Increased head circumference (in infants)
  • Sudden clumsiness, balance issues (ataxia), and localized neurological deficits: head tilt, vision changes, cranial nerve palsy, seizures, personality changes, declining school performance
Tumor types, organized clearly
📝 Note: how the slide’s tumor box is labeled
On the slide, the box titled “Medulloblastoma” actually lists facts that describe gliomas (glial precursor cells, astrocytoma, brainstem glioma, optic nerve glioma). The two are separate groups of tumors, organized correctly below.
TumorWhere / from whatKey facts
MedulloblastomaCerebellum (posterior fossa); from immature embryonal nerve cellsThe most common malignant childhood brain tumor. Fast-growing; can spread through the CSF to the spine. Causes ataxia (clumsy walking) and blocks CSF flow → increased ICP/hydrocephalus. Surgery + radiation + chemo.
Gliomas (the group)Arise from glial cells, the support cells of the brain and spinal cordIncludes the tumors below.
• AstrocytomaGlial cells called astrocytes; often the cerebellumThe most common type of glioma and the most common childhood brain tumor overall. Many are low-grade (slow-growing); surgery can be curative.
• Brainstem glioma (for example, DIPG)BrainstemCritically affects basic movement, breathing, and heart rate, plus cranial nerves (facial weakness, swallowing, eye movement). Peak ages 4–9. Usually inoperable; radiation; poor prognosis.
• Optic nerve gliomaOptic nerve/pathwayDirectly impairs vision (vision loss, bulging eye); linked with neurofibromatosis type 1.
Treatment and nursing care
  • Diagnosis: MRI (best), CT, biopsy; LP only if ICP isn’t high.
  • Treatment: surgery (most), radiation (avoided under age 3 if possible because it harms the developing brain), chemotherapy.
  • Post-op: neuro checks and vitals often; watch for increased ICP, bleeding, and CSF leak (clear drainage on the dressing; test for glucose); positioning per the surgeon (usually not flat on the back after posterior fossa surgery; side-lying, HOB flat or slightly up); watch for DI or SIADH; pain control; seizure precautions; fever can mean meningitis.
  • Posterior fossa syndrome (cerebellar mutism) can follow surgery: temporary loss of speech, irritability.
  • Family support, school re-entry, late effects (learning problems, growth/hormone issues).
💡 Exam tip
Morning headache + vomiting on waking + new clumsiness in a school-age child = think brain tumor (posterior fossa).
📚9.11 Other Neuro Conditions: Headache, AVM, SCI, Drowning & NeurotoxinsEngage Mod 10
ConditionWhat it isKey nursing points
HeadachesPrimary (migraine, tension, cluster) or secondary (from another cause: illness, injury, tumor). Migraine: throbbing, one-sided, light/sound sensitivity, nausea; may have aura. Tension: “tight band” around the head.Rule out a secondary cause first (red flags: worst-ever headache, waking from sleep, vomiting, neuro deficits). Headache diary; avoid triggers (poor sleep, dehydration, skipped meals, stress, screens, caffeine); ibuprofen or acetaminophen early, not more than a few days a week (rebound headaches).
Arteriovenous malformation (AVM)A congenital tangle of arteries connecting directly to veins without capillaries; can rupture and bleed.Signs: headaches, seizures, weakness; rupture = sudden severe headache, vomiting, decreased LOC (emergency). Treatment: surgery, endovascular embolization, or radiosurgery.
Spinal cord injury (SCI)Damage to the cord from trauma: complete (no function below the injury) or incomplete. Young children have flexible spines and heavy heads, so cervical injuries are common, sometimes without x-ray findings.Immobilize the spine first (cervical collar, log roll). Watch for spinal shock and breathing problems with high cervical injuries. Later: autonomic dysreflexia (injury at T6 or above: sudden high BP, headache, flushing, from a full bladder or bowel; sit up, find and remove the trigger). Rehab, skin care, bladder/bowel programs.
DrowningThe third leading cause of injury death worldwide; highest at ages 1–4 and in teens. Brain damage from hypoxia.Prevention: constant supervision near any water (even buckets and tubs), pool fencing, life jackets, swim lessons from age 1–4. Rescue: airway and breathing first, CPR, warm the child, hospital observation even if they seem fine (delayed respiratory distress).
TetanusToxin from Clostridium tetani spores (soil, rust, animal feces) entering a wound → painful muscle spasms, lockjaw (trismus), rigidity.Prevention: DTaP/Tdap vaccines, booster for dirty wounds. Treatment: tetanus immune globulin (TIG), wound cleaning, antibiotics (metronidazole), muscle relaxants such as diazepam; quiet, dark room to limit spasm triggers.
BotulismToxin from Clostridium botulinum; infant botulism from spores in honey or soil.Infant signs: constipation first, weak cry, poor feeding/suck, “floppy baby” (descending weakness), drooping eyelids, sluggish pupils, breathing failure. Treatment: botulism immune globulin (BabyBIG), ventilator support. No honey before age 1.
RabiesViral encephalitis from an infected animal bite (bats are the most common U.S. source); nearly always fatal once symptoms appear.Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water right away, report the bite, and give post-exposure prophylaxis (rabies immune globulin + vaccine series). Any bat found in a sleeping child’s room = treat.
💡 Exam tip
No honey before age 1 (botulism). Suspected spine injury: immobilize before anything else (after airway). Drowning prevention: supervision.
🦴

Lecture 2: Neuromuscular & Musculoskeletal System

Immobilization · Fractures · DDH · Clubfoot · Spine · OI · CP · DMD · Engage Mod 9
🛌9.12 Immobilization: Effects on the Body & the FamilyNM slides 3–4

When a child can’t move (casts, traction, bed rest, paralysis), every body system breaks down. Children lose muscle and bone faster than adults because they’re still growing.

ChangeLeads toPrevention
Disuse atrophy of muscles and jointsLoss of joint mobility, contractures, weaknessROM exercises, PT, splints, early mobility
Decreased respiratory effortSecretion buildup, aspiration risk, pneumonia, atelectasisTurn every 2 hours, incentive spirometry/blow bubbles, cough and deep breathe
Decreased metabolism → catabolism (body breaks down its own protein)Negative nitrogen balance, poor healing, weight lossHigh-protein, high-calorie diet
Bone demineralization (calcium leaves bones)Osteoporosis and hypercalcemia → renal calculi (kidney stones)Weight-bearing as allowed, fluids, avoid excess calcium supplementation while immobile
Decreased venous returnDependent edema, orthostatic intolerance (dizzy when getting up), thrombus riskGradual position changes, leg exercises, hydration
Skin pressurePressure injuriesReposition frequently, pressure-reduction mattresses, skin checks
🧒 The child: sensory and perceptual deprivation
  • Decreased exposure to normal play
  • Impaired growth and development
  • Risk for developmental regression (a toilet-trained toddler may start wetting again)
  • Boredom, frustration, anger, depression
👪 The family: logistical strain
  • Disrupted coping skills and sleep deprivation
  • Financial strain and medical bills
  • Shifting attention away from siblings (sibling jealousy or neglect)
🎯 Nursing care goals (slide)
Reposition frequently, use pressure-reduction mattresses, encourage high-protein/high-calorie diets, and allow the child autonomy whenever possible (choices about food, schedule, activities). Provide age-appropriate play (bring the play to the bed), schoolwork, and visits from friends.
💡 Exam tip
Immobilized child at risk for kidney stones? → push fluids. At risk for pneumonia? → turn, cough, deep breathe/incentive spirometry. Best psychosocial intervention? → give choices (autonomy).
🩻9.13 Pediatric Fractures, Compartment Syndrome & CastsNM slides 5–7 · Textbook

Children’s bones are pliable (bendy), porous, and heal rapidly thanks to a thick, blood-rich periosteum. But damage to the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) at the ends of long bones can cause permanent angular deformity or limb shortening, so growth plate fractures need close follow-up.

FractureDescription
Plastic deformationThe bone bends but doesn’t break; may need surgery to straighten it
Buckle (torus)The bone bulges from compression (like a crushed soda can); common in the forearm (wrist) in children under 12 after a fall on an outstretched hand
GreenstickThe bone bends and splinters on one side without fully breaking, like a green twig; common under age 10
ComminutedThe bone breaks in at least two places (several fragments); usually larger bones like the femur from high force
ComplicatedSplinters damage surrounding tissues or blood vessels (nerves, organs)

A spiral fracture in a nonambulatory infant, multiple fractures in different healing stages, or a story that doesn’t fit the injury should raise concern for abuse (or a bone disorder such as osteogenesis imperfecta).

Compartment syndrome: a surgical emergency

Excessive swelling inside a closed muscle compartment (or under a tight cast) disrupts circulation and compresses nerves. Without immediate surgical intervention (fasciotomy) within hours, muscle and nerve die, causing permanent damage. Assess the 6 Ps:

PWhat you find
PainSevere and unrelieved by medication or repositioning, out of proportion to the injury, and worse with passive stretch: the earliest and most important sign
PulseWeak or absent distal to the site: a late and ominous sign
PallorDecreased blood flow; pale/cool skin, capillary refill over 2–3 seconds
ParesthesiaNumbness or tingling distal to the fracture
ParalysisInability to move the distal limb
PressureSkin/compartment feels tight and tense
🚑 Emergency action (slide)
For a suspected fracture: immobilize the limb, assess the 6 Ps, apply cold, elevate if possible, and prepare for immediate transport. For suspected compartment syndrome: notify the provider immediately, keep the limb at heart level (not elevated above it, which lowers blood flow further), and expect the cast to be bivalved (split) and fasciotomy.
Casts and splints (slide 7)
  • Application: a hard exterior for stability with a cushioned interior. A plaster cast feels warm as it sets (expected); handle a wet cast with the palms, not fingertips (prevents dents that cause pressure spots); a plaster cast takes 24–72 hours to dry, fiberglass dries fast.
  • Immediate monitoring: assess neurovascular status (the 6 Ps, cap refill, color, warmth, movement, sensation) strictly because of the edema risk; keep the extremity elevated and supported above heart level for the first 24–48 hours, plus ice.
  • Maintenance: assess skin integrity continuously; keep the cast dry; for itching, blow cool air with a hair dryer, never put objects (coat hangers) or powder/lotion inside; petal rough edges; report a foul odor, hot spot, or drainage (infection or pressure ulcer under the cast), or a cracked/wet cast; provide accessible toys to accommodate mobility limits.
  • Psychosocial: use distraction during application and provide reassurance during removal (the cast saw is loud and frightening, but it vibrates and won’t cut the skin; show the child first).
Traction, sprains, and osteomyelitis (textbook)

Traction uses pulleys and weights to pull a bone back into alignment and reduce muscle spasm: keep weights hanging freely, never lift or remove them, check pin sites and neurovascular status. Sprains (ligament injuries) are treated with RICE (rest, ice, compression with an elastic bandage, elevation). Osteomyelitis is a bone infection, most often from Staphylococcus aureus (risk with sickle cell disease and open fractures): fever, bone pain, limping, refusing to bear weight, local redness/swelling; elevated WBC, ESR, CRP; treated with weeks of IV antibiotics (often vancomycin) through a PICC line.

💡 Exam tip
Pain that isn’t relieved by opioids or elevation in a casted limb = compartment syndrome until proven otherwise; call the provider now. A missing pulse is late.
🦶9.14 Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) & ClubfootNM slides 8–9 · Textbook

In DDH, the head of the femur doesn’t fit properly into the acetabulum (hip socket), so the hip is unstable and can partially or fully dislocate. Risk factors: breech position, female sex, firstborn, family history, low amniotic fluid, and tight swaddling with legs straight (swaddle with hips bent and loose: “hip-healthy” swaddling).

🔍 Clinical signs
  • Asymmetry of gluteal and thigh folds (extra folds on the affected side)
  • Limited hip abduction (can’t spread the leg out to the side)
  • Positive Ortolani maneuver: abduct and lift → a “clunk” as the hip reduces back into the socket
  • Positive Barlow maneuver: adduct and push back → the hip dislocates
  • Older infants: shortened leg (positive Galeazzi/Allis sign: uneven knee heights); walking child: limp or waddling gait, Trendelenburg sign
🪢 Stepped treatment by age
  • 0–6 months: Pavlik harness, worn 23 hours a day, holding the hips flexed and abducted. Don’t adjust the straps at home; check the skin 2–3 times a day; put a diaper and thin cotton shirt/knee socks under the straps; gently massage under straps; no lotions or powder; sponge bathe only if told not to remove it.
  • 6–18 months: closed reduction (manipulated into place under anesthesia) and immobilization in a spica cast (body cast from the waist down).
  • Over 18 months: open reduction surgery, then casting.

Spica cast care: neurovascular checks, keep the cast clean and dry around the diaper area (tuck a small diaper inside the cast edges, change often), turn every 2 hours, never use the bar between the legs to lift, use a car seat made for spica casts, and offer age-appropriate play.

Congenital clubfoot (talipes equinovarus)

A complex deformity in which shortened tendons make the front of the foot turn inward and the heel point down. About 50% of cases are bilateral; males are 2 times more likely; associated with maternal smoking and breech birth (and family history). The affected foot and calf may stay slightly smaller.

  • 1. Initiation: begin treatment within the first 2 weeks of life, when ligaments are most flexible.
  • 2. Serial casting (Ponseti method): the physician gently stretches the foot and applies a new long-leg cast weekly (up to about 10 changes). Neurovascular checks of the toes, keep casts dry.
  • 3. Bracing: then a foot-abduction brace (boots on a bar) worn 23 hours a day at first, gradually reducing to nights and naps, for several years (often to about age 4). Adherence to bracing prevents relapse, the most common reason treatment fails.
  • 4. Surgical alternative: considered if casting fails, or for an Achilles tendon lengthening (tenotomy), often near the end of casting.
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (textbook)

Temporary loss of blood supply to the femoral head, which dies (avascular necrosis) and slowly remodels. Usually boys ages 4–10 (most 5–7). Signs: painless or mildly painful limp, hip or knee pain, limited motion. Treatment: rest from high-impact activity, PT, braces, sometimes surgery; younger children have better outcomes.

💡 Exam tip
Ortolani = Out-to-In (reduces); Barlow = Back-and-Out (dislocates). Pavlik harness = 23 hours a day, no strap adjusting at home. Clubfoot treatment starts in the first 2 weeks.
🔀9.15 Spinal Deformities: Scoliosis, Lordosis & KyphosisNM slide 10 · Textbook
DeformityWhat it is and how it looksTreatment
Scoliosis (lateral curve)A sideways S- or C-shaped curve with rotation: uneven shoulders, uneven waist/hips, one shoulder blade sticks out, rib hump when bending forward. The most common spinal deformity; idiopathic type peaks in early adolescence, more in girls.Screen with the Adams forward-bend test (bend at the waist, arms hanging, look for a rib hump). Curves under 25° are observed. Brace for 25–45° curves while still growing (worn about 18–23 hours a day under a T-shirt; it stops progression, not reverses it). Spinal fusion for severe curves (over 45–50°).
Lordosis (swayback)The spine curves inward too much, tipping backward and pushing the hips forward; in the cervical or lumbar region. Normal in toddlers.Bracing, physical therapy (core strengthening). Often resolves with growth.
Kyphosis (hunchback)The spine curves forward too much in the cervical/thoracic spine (rounded back). Postural kyphosis from slouching, or Scheuermann kyphosis (wedge-shaped vertebrae; rigid).Postural PT, exercises; back braces for growing children; surgery rarely.
Nursing care for bracing and spinal fusion
  • Brace teaching: wear as prescribed (adherence is the biggest challenge for teens; body image), wear a snug cotton T-shirt underneath, check skin for redness, loose clothing over it; it may be removed for bathing and sports per provider.
  • After spinal fusion: log-roll to keep the spine aligned, neurovascular checks of the legs (movement and sensation), PCA for pain, incentive spirometry, watch for ileus (bowel sounds), early ambulation, no bending or twisting for months.
  • Emotional support: involve teens in decisions, support groups, clothing tips.
💡 Exam tip
Scoliosis screening = Adams forward-bend test. Brace range = 25–45°. Post-fusion = log roll and leg neuro checks.
🥚9.16 Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) & Holistic CareNM slides 11–12 · Textbook

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), nicknamed brittle bone disease, is a rare hereditary connective tissue disorder (about 1 in 15,000–20,000 infants). Step 1: a genetic mutation disrupts the genes that control collagen (risk factor: family history). Step 2: the body makes too little collagen or defective collagen. Step 3: bones lack strength; fractures happen frequently, often under minimal stress, and newborns can fracture during birth.

🔎 Signs by body area
  • Head and face: triangular face; blue, gray, or purple sclerae (whites of the eyes); weak, discolored teeth (dentinogenesis imperfecta)
  • Ears: hearing loss from inner ear bone deformities (often by adolescence/adulthood)
  • Torso: barrel-shaped chest, scoliosis
  • Limbs: bowing of the legs, short stature, underdeveloped muscles, loose joints
  • Systemic complications: heart valve problems, severe respiratory infections, kidney stones
📊 Severity spectrum
  • Type I: mild and most common (about 50%); makes typical collagen but not enough; manageable fracture risk; normal height
  • Types III–VIII: moderate to severe; altered collagen; high fracture risk, severe bone deformities, altered growth, mobility limits
  • Type II: fatal at or shortly after birth (about 1 in 100,000): severe collagen problems, underdeveloped lungs, extreme fractures

Diagnosis: genetic testing (blood, saliva, or skin), skin biopsy to examine collagen structure, x-rays, bone scans, or hip bone biopsy to monitor development. Distinguishing OI from child abuse is important when a child has multiple fractures.

Assess & monitorTreat & protectEducate & support
Birth precautions: close monitoring during and after delivery. Routine screenings: vision and hearing; check for unexplained bruising and new fractures. Imaging and biopsies to monitor development.Protective equipment: prophylactic orthotics, splints, braces, casting to prevent injury, deformities, and contractures. Surgery (rods placed in long bones) for severe deformities. Tailored PT for safe strength building (swimming is ideal).Nutrition and weight: daily calcium and vitamin D (taken separately from ibandronate); healthy weight. Safe play: avoid high-impact activities; PT guides safe, enjoyable play. Psychosocial health: fragility and appearance take a toll; watch for low self-esteem and depression; mental health support for client and caregivers.
💊 Rx alert: ibandronate (a bisphosphonate)
Action: reduces bone turnover and slows bone loss, increasing bone density. Rules: take with a full glass of water (plain water only, on an empty stomach first thing in the morning), and the client must remain upright for at least 60 minutes (prevents esophageal irritation/ulcers; no food or other meds during that time). Contraindications: low calcium, severe kidney problems, esophageal issues. Alert: risk of jaw osteonecrosis (good dental care) and atypical thigh-bone fractures; avoid excessive alcohol.
Handling a child with OI
  • Lift by supporting the buttocks and the shoulders/head with open hands; never lift an infant by the ankles to change a diaper (slide the hips up with a hand under the buttocks).
  • Take blood pressure gently (manual cuff, no automatic cuffs that squeeze hard); handle gently during baths and dressing.
  • Padded, safe environment; protective gear; teach parents how to recognize fractures; genetic counseling.
💡 Exam tip
Infant with blue sclerae and multiple fractures = OI. Ibandronate = full glass of water, upright 60 minutes. Diaper change = lift by the buttocks, not the ankles.
🧩9.17 Restorative Mobility (PT/OT) & Cerebral PalsyNM slides 13–15 · Textbook

The ultimate goal of every intervention is returning the child to a life of active, independent play.

🚶 Physical therapy (PT)
Focus: gross motor dysfunction and restorative mobility (walking, balance, strength). Interventions: assessing the need for mobility equipment (wheelchairs, walkers, crutches) and educating the family on daily use.
✋ Occupational therapy (OT)
Focus: fine motor dysfunction and daily occupations (the “jobs” of daily life). Interventions: promoting independence in play skills and ADLs (activities of daily living); prescribing adaptive equipment for feeding, dressing, bathing, and toileting.
Cerebral palsy (CP)

CP is a non-progressive neuromuscular disorder caused by brain damage or developmental defects affecting motor function (movement, posture, tone). The brain injury doesn’t get worse, but the effects on muscles and bones (contractures, hip dislocation, scoliosis) can change as the child grows. 70–80% of cases are due to unknown prenatal factors.

TimingRisk factors
PrenatalMaternal infections, malnutrition, toxins, genetic abnormalities
PerinatalAsphyxia/anoxic injury, low birth weight and prematurity (the biggest risk), meconium aspiration, prolonged labor
PostnatalBrain injury, childhood infections (meningitis), stroke, shaken baby syndrome (abusive head trauma), near-drowning
🏃 Motor findings
  • Delayed gross motor development (not sitting by 8 months, not walking by 18 months)
  • Abnormal crawling (asymmetric, “commando” crawl)
  • Consistent tongue thrusting and poor sucking; feeding difficulties
  • Early hand preference (before 12–18 months suggests weakness on the other side)
  • Toe walking
🔁 Reflex and posture findings
  • Persistent primitive reflexes (Moro, tonic neck) beyond the expected age
  • Hyperreflexia and clonus
  • Rigid posture with arching of the back (opisthotonos)
  • Scissoring (legs cross) and stiff extension of the legs

Associated disabilities: seizures and behavioral issues; sensory impairments (vision, speech, hearing); altered learning and reasoning (note: 50–60% have normal intelligence despite severe physical limitations, so never assume a child who can’t speak doesn’t understand); bowel, bladder (constipation), and dental concerns; aspiration risk.

TypeBrain areaTone and movement
Spastic (pyramidal): about 80%Cerebral cortex (motor cortex)Hypertonicity (severe muscle tightness), increased deep tendon reflexes, clonus. Crouched gait with rigid scissoring; positive Babinski reflex. Can be hemiplegia (one side), diplegia (mostly legs), or quadriplegia (all four limbs).
Dyskinetic (extrapyramidal)Basal gangliaAthetoid: slow, writhing, wormlike involuntary movements of the extremities, trunk, neck, face. Dystonic: slow twisting movements, abnormal postures from muscle contractions, severe drooling and speech impairment. Movements increase with stress and disappear in sleep.
Ataxic (extrapyramidal)CerebellumPoor balance and coordination; wide-based, unsteady gait; intention tremors; can’t do rapid repetitive or purposeful movements well.
Therapeutic management core (slide 15)
  • Pharmacological: baclofen (muscle relaxant for spasticity, oral or by an implanted intrathecal pump; never stop abruptly: withdrawal can cause high fever, seizures, and rebound spasticity), diazepam (Valium) for spasms, botulinum toxin (Botox) injections into tight muscles for severe spasms, and AEDs for seizures.
  • Interdisciplinary: PT, OT, speech therapy, mobilizing devices (braces/orthotics, walkers, wheelchairs), augmented communication devices, dietitian (high-calorie needs, feeding tubes if aspirating), orthopedic surgery for contractures.
  • Nursing: safety and fall prevention, aspiration precautions (upright feeding, thickened liquids per speech therapy), adequate calories, skin care, bowel program, dental care, promote independence and school inclusion.
💡 Exam tip
Scissoring + hypertonia + positive Babinski = spastic CP (cortex). Writhing = dyskinetic (basal ganglia). Wide-based gait = ataxic (cerebellum). Biggest risk factor = prematurity/low birth weight.
💪9.18 Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) & Holistic Psychosocial CareNM slides 16–17 · Textbook

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an inherited X-linked recessive disorder (almost always boys; mothers are carriers) in which the body can’t make dystrophin, a protein that holds muscle cells together. Muscles break down, causing progressive, rapid degeneration of symmetric skeletal muscle groups, starting in the hips and thighs.

Diagnostics: elevated blood creatine kinase (CK), an enzyme that leaks from damaged muscle, high even before clinical signs; blood PCR for the dystrophin gene mutation; and muscle biopsy (absent dystrophin).

PhaseAgeWhat happens
Phase 1 (onset)Ages 3–5Fatigue and lower-extremity weakness, delayed motor skills, unsteady, waddling gait, frequent falls, trouble climbing stairs
Phase 2Mid-childhoodGowers sign: to stand up from the floor, the child “walks” his hands up his own legs; frequent falling; calf pseudohypertrophy (calves look big and strong, but muscle is being replaced by fat and scar tissue)
Phase 3Age 12+Progressive difficulty walking leading to total loss of ambulation (wheelchair); atrophy spreads to the face, chest, and neck; scoliosis and contractures
Phase 4 (late stage)Late teens–adulthoodSevere progressive respiratory compromise (weak breathing muscles, high pneumonia risk) and cardiac difficulties (cardiomyopathy). Life expectancy is typically 15–30 years (per the slide); respiratory or cardiac failure is the usual cause of death.

Treatment (no cure): corticosteroids (prednisone or deflazacort) to slow muscle loss, PT and stretching to delay contractures, braces and wheelchairs, respiratory support (cough assist, BiPAP), cardiac monitoring, spinal surgery for scoliosis, newer gene-based therapies. Prevent obesity (harder to move), keep active as long as possible, and prevent respiratory infection (vaccines, airway clearance).

AreaWhat the nurse does
Promoting independenceIndividualize care based on developmental level, not chronological age. Encourage self-care and ADLs for as long as physically possible (vital for MD and spina bifida). Help the child keep a positive self-image.
School, play, and socializationFacilitate integration into school and educate peers to prevent bullying. Create specific safety plans for recreation: strict seizure precautions around water and driving, and bans on contact sports for children with VP shunts.
Adaptive communicationUse augmented communication devices (electronic touch screens, picture boards) for CP and developmental delays. Always communicate directly with the child while supporting the parents.
Family support and palliative needsCoordinate extensive interdisciplinary care (PT, OT, neurology, dietitians). Provide genetic counseling resources (especially for MD and spina bifida). Facilitate long-term care and end-of-life discussions gracefully when appropriate; respite care for caregivers.
💡 Exam tip
Gowers sign + big calves + boy age 3–5 + high CK = DMD. Late-stage priority = respiratory (pneumonia) and cardiac function. Speak to the child directly.

💡 Mnemonics & Memory Aids

Every memory trick from the study sheet in one place, organized by module, for a quick review the night before.

Module 7: Immune & Heme

🩸 “Everything low but TIBC”

7.2 IDA labs

Hgb, Hct, ferritin, serum iron, MCV, MCH, MCHC all ↓; TIBC ↑.

🍊 Iron teaching: “Juice, Straw, Black, Lock”

7.3 Iron

Give with juice (vitamin C), not milk · use a straw/dropper to the back of the mouth · black stools are expected · lock it up (poisoning).

🥛 “A quart is the cap”

7.3 Milk

Slide: limit milk to 1 quart (32 oz) a day so it doesn’t replace iron-rich foods.

🎄 Hemophilia A vs. B: “A = 8, B = 9 (Christmas)”

7.4 Types

A = factor VIII (80%, classic) · B = factor IX (Christmas disease) · vWD = von Willebrand factor, affects both sexes.

🧊 Joint bleed: “Factor + RICE”

7.5 Hemophilia

Give factor first, then Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Pressure 15+ minutes. No aspirin/NSAIDs.

⏱️ Hemophilia labs: “Only the PTT is late”

7.5 Diagnosis

PTT prolonged; platelets, PT, fibrinogen normal.

💧 Sickle cell triggers: “Dry, Cold, High, Sick, Stressed”

7.6 SCD

Dry (dehydration) · Cold · High altitude · Sick (infection/fever) · Stressed (emotional or strenuous activity).

🔥 VOC care: “HOP” — Hydrate, Oxygen (if low), Pain meds

7.8 SCD care

Plus warmth, never ice, bed rest, I&O, daily weights.

🫀 Crisis match: “Pain, Pool, Pause, Puff”

7.7 Crises

Pain = vaso-occlusive · Pool = sequestration (big spleen, shock, 6 mo–4 yr) · Pause = aplastic (marrow pauses, parvovirus) · Puff = acute chest syndrome.

🎗️ Leukemia: “Anemia, Bleeding, Infection” (ABI)

7.9 Leukemia

Anemia = pale and tired · Bleeding = low platelets (bruises, petechiae) · Infection = no mature WBCs (fever). Plus bone pain.

🧮 ANC: “WBC × (segs + bands) ÷ 100”

7.10 Neutropenia

Under 500 = severe, protective precautions. Fever + neutropenia = antibiotics fast.

👶 HIV testing: “Under 18 months = PCR”

7.11 HIV

Mom’s antibodies linger up to 18 months, so test for the virus (PCR). Over 18 months: ELISA + Western blot (slide).

💉 Anaphylaxis: “Epi first, ask later”

7.12 Allergy

Epinephrine IM thigh immediately; antihistamines and albuterol are second-line.

🦋 SLE: “Butterfly hates the sun”

7.13 SLE

Malar rash + photosensitivity → SPF 50+, hats, protective clothing.

🩸 “Low alone = ITP; low all = aplastic; clot and bleed = DIC”

7.14 Other disorders

Quick way to tell the three apart.

Module 8: Genitourinary

🚽 Girls’ UTI risk: “Short and close”

8.5 UTI

Short urethra, close to the anus.

🧼 UTI prevention: “Front, Fluids, Flow, Fiber, Finish”

8.6 UTI

Wipe front to back · lots of fluids · don’t hold the flow (void often) · fiber for constipation · finish the antibiotic. Plus no bubble baths, cotton underwear.

⬇️ “Hypo = below, Epi = on top”

8.3 Spadias

Hypospadias = underside (ventral) · Epispadias = top (dorsal). No circumcision — save the foreskin.

🔵 Cryptorchidism: “Pexy prevents, Self-exam protects”

8.4 Orchiopexy

Orchipexy 6–24 months preserves fertility and lowers cancer risk; teach testicular self-exam.

↩️ VUR grades: “1–2 watch, 3–4 pills + pictures, 4–5 surgery”

8.7 VUR

Mild = observe · moderate = prophylactic antibiotics + VCUG · severe with UTIs = surgery.

🎈 Nephrotic: “Protein OUT, fluid IN”

8.8 Nephrotic

Massive proteinuria, low albumin, high lipids, big edema, normal BP, age 2–7, prednisone.

🫖 APSGN: “Strep, then Cola and Pressure”

8.9 APSGN

Strep 10–14 days earlier → cola-colored urine + high blood pressure, peak age 7. Supportive care.

✋ Wilms: “Hands off the belly”

8.10 Wilms

Never palpate the abdomen.

Module 9: Neuro, NM & MSK

🔟 GCS: “Eyes 4, Verbal 5, Motor 6 — 8 means intubate”

9.1 GCS

Max 15, min 3. ≤8 = coma; airway at risk.

🌅 Infant ICP: “Bulge, Cry, Grow, Sunset”

9.2 ICP

Bulging fontanel · high-pitched cry · head grows · sunset eyes. Late: bradycardia, posturing, fixed pupils.

🚑 “Epidural = arterial = express”

9.3 TBI

Epidural bleeds expand fast (lucid interval). Subdural = venous = most common, slower.

🦵 Meningeal signs: “Brudzinski = Bend neck; Kernig = Knee”

9.4 Meningitis

Brudzinski: bend the neck → hips/knees flex. Kernig: extend the knee → pain.

🧫 Bacterial CSF: “Cloudy, Climbing protein, Crashing glucose”

9.4 CSF

Viral is clear with normal glucose.

😷 Meningitis: “Droplet first, 24 after”

9.5 Meningitis

Droplet precautions on suspicion; keep for 24 hours after antibiotics. Purple rash = emergency.

🌡️ Febrile seizure: “Fast rise, under 5, peak at 2, Tylenol for comfort”

9.6 Febrile

Antipyretics don’t prevent seizures.

🛟 Seizure care: “Side, Safe, Silent mouth, Stopwatch”

9.7 Seizures

Turn to side · make area safe · nothing in the mouth · time it. 5 minutes = Diastat.

🧠 Shunt trouble: “Headache, Grades, Mood”

9.8 VP shunt

Subtle signs of malfunction in school-age kids: headaches, falling grades, behavior/mood changes. Infection risk highest month 1.

🎗️ Myelomeningocele: “Prone, Moist, Latex-free, Close in 72”

9.9 Spina bifida

Prone position · sterile moist dressing · latex precautions · surgery within 12–72 hours. Prevention: folic acid 400 mcg.

🌄 Brain tumor: “Morning headache, Morning vomit, Messy walking”

9.10 Tumors

Posterior fossa tumors cause ataxia. Medulloblastoma = cerebellum; astrocytoma = most common glioma.

🍯 “No honey before one”

9.11 Botulism

Infant botulism: constipation first, then floppy baby.

⚠️ The 6 Ps

9.13 Compartment syndrome

Pain (first, unrelieved) · Pulse (late) · Pallor · Paresthesia · Paralysis · Pressure.

🦴 Fractures: “Bend, Bulge, Bark, Bits”

9.13 Fractures

Bend = plastic deformation · Bulge = buckle · Bark (green twig) = greenstick · Bits = comminuted.

🦵 “Ortolani = Out-to-In (reduces); Barlow = Back-and-Out (dislocates)”

9.14 DDH

Pavlik harness 0–6 months, 23 hours a day.

📐 Scoliosis brace: “25 to 45, brace to survive”

9.15 Spine

Brace 25–45°; over 45–50° = fusion; screen with Adams forward bend.

💙 OI: “Blue eyes, Broken bones, Bad hearing”

9.16 OI

Blue sclerae, fractures, hearing loss. Ibandronate: water + upright 60 minutes. Lift by the buttocks.

🧩 CP types: “Spastic = Stiff (Cortex), Dyskinetic = Dance (Basal ganglia), Ataxic = Atilt (Cerebellum)”

9.17 CP

Spastic ~80%: scissoring, +Babinski.

💪 DMD: “Gowers, Giant calves, Guys, Gone by teens”

9.18 DMD

Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, boys (X-linked), wheelchair by about 12; high CK.
